title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: The environment, and its exact answers
text:
The environment, and its exact answers
We use the same \(4\times4\) gridworld: terminal corners 0 and 15, four deterministic moves, \(-1\) per step until termination, undiscounted (\(\gamma=1\)). We rebuild the tensors \(P[s,a,s']\) and \(R[s,a,s']\), but from here on they play two very different roles:

the simulator uses them to generate experience (this is “the environment”), and
the DP oracle uses them to compute exact values we compare MC against.

The Monte Carlo algorithms themselves touch neither - they only ever see \((S_t, A_t, R_{t+1})\) triples.
We start with the grid’s fixed facts: sixteen states, four actions, the two absorbing corners, and the action codes we will print as arrows.

n_states, n_actions = 16, 4
TERMINAL_STATES = [0, 15]
terminal = np.zeros(n_states, dtype=bool)
terminal[TERMINAL_STATES] = True
UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT = 0, 1, 2, 3
ARROWS = {UP: "^", DOWN: "v", LEFT: "<", RIGHT: ">"}
GRID_SHAPE = (4, 4) # (n_rows, n_cols) of the gridworld
STEP_REWARD_GRID = -1.0 # reward on every step out of a non-terminal state

Plain-Python helpers: grid_step is the deterministic dynamics we are about to bake into \(P\), while values_figure and policy_figure draw a length-16 vector as a \(4\times4\) grid so we can eyeball values and greedy actions as we go.

def grid_step(s, a):
    """Return the state that action `a` leads to from state `s`.

    Moves are deterministic. A move that would step off the grid leaves the agent where it is,
    and a terminal state is absorbing: every action leaves the agent in it.

    Parameters
    ----------
    s : int
        The current state, numbered ``row * n_cols + col`` on the grid.
    a : {UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT}
        The action.

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The next state.
    """
    if s in TERMINAL_STATES:
        return s
    n_rows, n_cols = GRID_SHAPE
    row, col = divmod(s, n_cols)
    if a == UP: row = max(row - 1, 0)
    elif a == DOWN: row = min(row + 1, n_rows - 1)
    elif a == LEFT: col = max(col - 1, 0)
    elif a == RIGHT: col = min(col + 1, n_cols - 1)
    return row * n_cols + col


STEP = {UP: (0, 1), DOWN: (0, -1), LEFT: (-1, 0), RIGHT: (1, 0)} # action -> (dx, dy) when drawn

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GridTheme:
    template: str    # plotly template
    background: str  # plot background, which shows in the gaps between cells
    floor: str       # fill of a non-terminal cell

GRID_LIGHT = GridTheme(template="plotly_white", background="white", floor="#f2f2f2")
GRID_DARK = GridTheme(template="plotly_dark", background="black", floor="#9e9d9d")
GRID_TERMINAL = colors[4] # terminal cell fill, the same in both themes
GRID_INK, GRID_ARROW = "#4a4a4a", colors[2] # labels and policy arrows, drawn on the cells in both themes

def grid_xy(s, shape):
    """Convert a state id to (x, y) plot coordinates, with grid row 0 drawn at the top.

    Parameters
    ----------
    s : int
        The state, numbered ``row * n_cols + col``.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).

    Returns
    -------
    x, y : int
        The column, and the row counted up from the bottom.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    row, col = divmod(int(s), n_cols)
    return col, n_rows - 1 - row

def grid_panels(panel_titles, shape, title="", n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=100, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Make an empty figure with one subplot per panel, each holding a grid of square cells.

    The figure is tall enough for every cell to be ``cell_px`` pixels high and takes the page
    width; the cells stay square. The panels are laid out left to right, then top to bottom.

    Parameters
    ----------
    panel_titles : list of str
        One title per panel.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The (n_rows, n_cols) of the grid. Every panel shares it.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title. Plotly HTML (<b>, <br>, <sup>) works.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 100
        Height of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The plotly template and plot background. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        The figure, with the axes of every panel hidden and scaled so the cells are square.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    n_panels = len(panel_titles)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or n_panels
    n_panel_rows = -(-n_panels // n_panel_cols) # ceiling division
    gap_x_px, gap_y_px = 20, 40 # between panels
    plot_width = n_panel_cols * n_cols * cell_px + (n_panel_cols - 1) * gap_x_px
    plot_height = n_panel_rows * n_rows * cell_px + (n_panel_rows - 1) * gap_y_px

    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=n_panel_rows,
        cols=n_panel_cols,
        subplot_titles=[f"<b>{t}</b>" for t in panel_titles],
        horizontal_spacing=gap_x_px / plot_width,
        vertical_spacing=gap_y_px / plot_height
    )

    for row in range(1, n_panel_rows + 1):
        for col in range(1, n_panel_cols + 1):
            x_axis = fig.get_subplot(row, col).xaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
            fig.update_xaxes(range=[-0.55, n_cols - 0.45], visible=False, constrain="domain",
                             row=row, col=col)
            fig.update_yaxes(range=[-0.55, n_rows - 0.45], visible=False, scaleanchor=x_axis,
                             constrain="domain", row=row, col=col)

    margin = dict(l=10, r=10, b=10, t=(80 if title else 0) + 30)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=title,
        height=plot_height + margin["t"] + margin["b"],
        margin=margin,
        template=theme.template,
        plot_bgcolor=theme.background,
        showlegend=False
    )
    return fig

def draw_cells(fig, shape, fills, labels, row=1, col=1, pad=0.04):
    """Draw one filled square per state into a subplot, with an optional label on top.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fig : plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        A figure from `grid_panels`. It is changed in place.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).
    fills : list of str, length n_rows * n_cols
        The fill color of each state's cell.
    labels : dict of {int: str}
        Text drawn in the middle of a cell, by state, e.g. ``{0: "T"}``.
    row, col : int, default 1, 1
        The panel to draw into.
    pad : float, default 0.04
        Gap around each cell, in cell widths.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    for s in range(n_rows * n_cols):
        x, y = grid_xy(s, shape)
        fig.add_shape(
            type="rect",
            x0=x - 0.5 + pad,
            x1=x + 0.5 - pad,
            y0=y - 0.5 + pad,
            y1=y + 0.5 - pad,
            fillcolor=fills[s],
            line_width=0,
            layer="below",
            row=row, col=col
        )
    for s, label in labels.items():
        x, y = grid_xy(s, shape)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y, text=f"<b>{label}</b>", showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=14, color=GRID_INK), row=row, col=col)

def draw_arrows(fig, shape, actions, states, row=1, col=1, color=GRID_ARROW):
    """Draw an arrow in each of the given states, pointing the way its action moves.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fig : plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        A figure from `grid_panels`. It is changed in place.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).
    actions : array_like of int, shape (n_rows * n_cols,)
        The action in each state. Only the entries for ``states`` are drawn.
    states : array_like of int
        The states that get an arrow.
    row, col : int, default 1, 1
        The panel to draw into.
    color : str, default GRID_ARROW
        The arrow color.
    """
    subplot = fig.get_subplot(row, col)
    x_ref = subplot.xaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
    y_ref = subplot.yaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
    for s in states:
        x, y = grid_xy(s, shape)
        dx, dy = STEP[int(actions[s])]
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=x + 0.34 * dx,
            y=y + 0.34 * dy,
            ax=x - 0.22 * dx,
            ay=y - 0.22 * dy,
            xref=x_ref, yref=y_ref,
            axref=x_ref, ayref=y_ref,
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=2, arrowsize=1.0, arrowwidth=2.2, arrowcolor=color
        )

def values_figure(values, shape, title="", fmt=".1f", n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=100, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Draw one number per state, laid out as the grid and colored by size.

    Each panel has its own color scale, so the colors compare states within a panel; the printed
    numbers carry the values.

    Parameters
    ----------
    values : dict of {str: array_like of shape (n_rows * n_cols,)}
        One panel per entry: its title, and the number for each state (e.g. a state-value
        function).
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title.
    fmt : str, default ".1f"
        d3 format spec for the numbers printed in the cells.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 100
        Height of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The plotly template and plot background. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    fig = grid_panels(list(values), shape, title, n_panel_cols, cell_px, theme)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or len(values)
    for i, v in enumerate(values.values()):
        grid = np.asarray(v, dtype=float).reshape(n_rows, n_cols)
        state = np.arange(n_rows * n_cols).reshape(n_rows, n_cols)
        fig.add_heatmap(
            x=np.arange(n_cols),
            y=np.arange(n_rows),
            z=grid[::-1], # grid row 0 at the top
            customdata=state[::-1],
            colorscale="Teal",
            showscale=False,
            texttemplate=f"%{{z:{fmt}}}",
            xgap=3,
            ygap=3,
            hovertemplate=f"state %{{customdata}}: <b>%{{z:{fmt}}}</b><extra></extra>",
            row=i // n_panel_cols + 1, col=i % n_panel_cols + 1
        )
    return fig

def policy_figure(policies, shape, terminal, title="", n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=100, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Draw one arrow per state for each deterministic policy, laid out as the grid.

    Terminal states are the terminal color and labeled "T"; every other state gets an arrow.

    Parameters
    ----------
    policies : dict of {str: array_like of int, shape (n_rows * n_cols,)}
        One panel per entry: its title, and the action taken in each state.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).
    terminal : ndarray of bool, shape (n_rows * n_cols,)
        True for the terminal states.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 100
        Height of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The template, background and floor fill. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    fills = [GRID_TERMINAL if terminal[s] else theme.floor for s in range(n_rows * n_cols)]
    labels = {int(s): "T" for s in np.flatnonzero(terminal)}
    fig = grid_panels(list(policies), shape, title, n_panel_cols, cell_px, theme)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or len(policies)
    for i, actions in enumerate(policies.values()):
        row, col = i // n_panel_cols + 1, i % n_panel_cols + 1
        draw_cells(fig, shape, fills, labels, row, col)
        draw_arrows(fig, shape, actions, np.flatnonzero(~terminal), row, col)
    return fig

Filling \(P\) and \(R\) is one pass over every \((s, a)\) pair. The moves are deterministic, so exactly one entry of \(P[s,a,\cdot]\) is \(1\), and every step taken out of a non-terminal state earns \(-1\).

P = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states)) # p(s' | s, a)
reward_table = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states)) # r(s, a, s')
for s in range(n_states):
    for a in range(n_actions):
        s_next = grid_step(s, a)
        P[s, a, s_next] = 1.0
        if s not in TERMINAL_STATES:
            reward_table[s, a, s_next] = STEP_REWARD_GRID

The same arrays again as PyTensor constants, together with the expected one-step reward \(r(s,a) = \sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,a)\, r(s,a,s')\) and a symbolic \(\gamma\). Both the oracle and the simulator are built out of these.

P_sym = pt.as_tensor_variable(P)
reward_sym = pt.as_tensor_variable(reward_table)
not_terminal = pt.as_tensor_variable((~terminal).astype("float64"))
reward_mean = (P_sym * reward_sym).sum(axis=2) # r(s, a), the expected one-step reward
gamma_sym = pt.scalar("gamma")

The oracle is the policy-evaluation scan from the Dynamic Programming chapter: 600 sweeps of the expectation backup drive any policy’s \(v_\pi\) to convergence. A second compiled function turns a state-value vector into action values with one lookahead through the model, which is how we get \(q_\pi\).

# the DP oracle: exact v_pi and q_pi for any policy
pi_eval_sym = pt.matrix("pi")
P_pi = (pi_eval_sym[:, :, None] * P_sym).sum(axis=1) # p(s' | s) under pi
reward_pi = (pi_eval_sym * reward_mean).sum(axis=1)  # r(s) under pi

def evaluation_step(v_prev, reward_pi, P_pi, gamma, not_terminal):
    """One sweep of iterative policy evaluation on the collapsed Markov reward process.

    Applies the Bellman expectation backup to every state at once,

        v_{k+1}(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) sum_s' p(s'|s, a) [ r(s, a, s') + gamma * v_k(s') ],

    which, with the policy folded into ``reward_pi`` and ``P_pi``, is the linear map
    ``v_{k+1} = r^pi + gamma * P^pi v_k``. Here every reward is -1 until a terminal state is
    reached, and ``not_terminal`` pins the two terminal states to 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    v_prev : TensorVariable, shape (n_states,)
        The values v_k from the previous sweep.
    reward_pi : TensorVariable, shape (n_states,)
        Expected one-step reward under pi, ``r^pi(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) r(s, a)``.
    P_pi : TensorVariable, shape (n_states, n_states)
        State-to-state transition matrix under pi, ``P^pi[s, s'] = sum_a pi(a|s) p(s'|s, a)``.
    gamma : TensorVariable, scalar
        Discount factor.
    not_terminal : TensorVariable, shape (n_states,)
        1.0 for a non-terminal state, 0.0 for a terminal one.

    Returns
    -------
    TensorVariable, shape (n_states,)
        The values v_{k+1}.
    """
    return not_terminal * (reward_pi + gamma * pt.dot(P_pi, v_prev))

v_eval = pytensor.scan(
    fn=evaluation_step,
    outputs_info=pt.zeros((n_states,)),
    non_sequences=[reward_pi, P_pi, gamma_sym, not_terminal],
    n_steps=600,
    return_updates=False,
)
evaluate_policy = pytensor.function([pi_eval_sym, gamma_sym], v_eval[-1])

v_sym = pt.vector("v")
action_values_of = pytensor.function(
    [v_sym, gamma_sym],
    (P_sym * (reward_sym + gamma_sym * v_sym[None, None, :])).sum(axis=2)
)

Policy improvement, also unchanged from the DP chapter: score every action by one-step lookahead and put all of the probability mass on the best one.

def greedy_from_values(v, gamma):
    """Return the deterministic greedy policy of a state-value function, via one-step lookahead.

    Looks one step ahead through the model with the compiled ``action_values_of``,

        q(s, a) = sum_s' p(s'|s, a) [ r(s, a, s') + gamma * v(s') ],

    and picks ``argmax_a q(s, a)`` in every state. Ties go to the lowest-numbered action.

    Parameters
    ----------
    v : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        State values v(s).
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.

    Returns
    -------
    pi_greedy : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The policy as a one-hot matrix: 1.0 on the greedy action of each state, 0.0 elsewhere.
    a_greedy : ndarray of int, shape (n_states,)
        The greedy action of each state.
    """
    a_greedy = action_values_of(v, gamma).argmax(axis=1)
    pi_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    pi_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_greedy] = 1.0
    return pi_greedy, a_greedy

Running the oracle on the equiprobable random policy at \(\gamma = 1\) gives the two prediction references, \(v_\pi\) and \(q_\pi\), with the terminal rows pinned to zero.

# exact answers we will test against
GAMMA_GRID = 1.0
pi_random = np.ones((n_states, n_actions)) / n_actions
v_pi_random = evaluate_policy(pi_random, GAMMA_GRID)
q_pi_random = action_values_of(v_pi_random, GAMMA_GRID)
q_pi_random[terminal] = 0.0
pi_star = pi_random

Policy iteration - alternating evaluation and greedification until the policy stops changing - gives the control references \(v_*\) and \(q_*\). Printing both value functions fixes the targets everything below has to converge to.

for _ in range(50): # policy iteration
    pi_new, a_star = greedy_from_values(evaluate_policy(pi_star, GAMMA_GRID), GAMMA_GRID)
    if np.array_equal(pi_new, pi_star):
        break
    pi_star = pi_new
v_star = evaluate_policy(pi_star, GAMMA_GRID)
q_star = action_values_of(v_star, GAMMA_GRID)
q_star[terminal] = 0.0


values_figure(
    {"Exact v<sub>π</sub> (equiprobable random policy)": v_pi_random,
     "Exact v<sub>*</sub>": v_star},
    GRID_SHAPE
).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            



values_figure(
    {"Exact v<sub>π</sub> (equiprobable random policy)": v_pi_random,
     "Exact v<sub>*</sub>": v_star},
    GRID_SHAPE,
    theme=GRID_DARK
).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: Simulating episodes with scan and a threaded RNG
text:
Simulating episodes with scan and a threaded RNG
Everything below consumes batches of episodes, so we build one compiled simulator that rolls out \(B\) episodes in parallel: the recurrent state of the scan is a length-\(B\) vector of current states, and each step samples \(A_t \sim \pi(\cdot\mid S_t)\) and \(S_{t+1} \sim p(\cdot\mid S_t, A_t)\) with batched categorical draws.
Two PyTensor mechanics are worth calling out:








Mechanic
What it does
Why it matters




RNG threading
In PyTensor’s random API every draw consumes an RNG state and returns a fresh one: rng, a = rng.categorical(p=...). Inside scan we make the RNG one of the recurrent outputs, so scan hands back the final RNG state, which we register in updates=.
That write is what makes consecutive calls of the compiled function continue the stream instead of replaying it.


Fixed-length padding
scan wants a fixed number of steps, but episodes end at random times. The terminal states are absorbing with reward 0, so we just keep “playing” after termination.
The padded steps add nothing to any return, and we mask them out of the statistics with not_terminal.



The rollout gives aligned tensors \(S, A, R\) of shape \((T, B)\) where row \(t\) holds the triple \((S_t, A_t, R_{t+1})\). Returns come from one more backwards scan, \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1}\), and sample averages from a scatter-add (inc_subtensor, which accumulates over repeated indices).

rng_simulate = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=2026, name="rng_simulate")
pi_rollout_sym = pt.matrix("pi")   # policy to roll out, (n_states, n_actions)
s_start_sym = pt.lvector("s0")     # (n_episodes,) start states
a_start_sym = pt.lvector("a0")     # (n_episodes,) forced first actions (for exploring starts)
max_steps_sym = pt.iscalar("T")    # episode length cap

def simulate_step(s, rng, pi, P):
    """Advance every episode in the batch by one time step.

    Samples an action from the policy, then the next state from the model,

        A_t ~ pi(. | S_t),    S_{t+1} ~ p(. | S_t, A_t),

    and returns the reward ``R_{t+1} = r(S_t, A_t)``, the expected one-step reward. The moves
    are deterministic here, so that is exactly the reward the move earns: -1 out of a
    non-terminal state, 0 out of a terminal one. Terminal states absorb, so an episode that has
    ended keeps sitting in its terminal state, earning 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    s : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_episodes,)
        The current states S_t.
    rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
        The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
    pi : TensorVariable, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The policy being rolled out, pi(a|s).
    P : TensorVariable, shape (n_states, n_actions, n_states)
        Transition probabilities p(s'|s, a).

    Returns
    -------
    s_next : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_episodes,)
        The next states S_{t+1}.
    rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
        The advanced generator.
    a : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_episodes,)
        The actions A_t.
    reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_episodes,)
        The rewards R_{t+1}.
    """
    rng, a = rng.categorical(p=pi[s]) # A_t ~ pi(.|S_t), batched over episodes
    rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a]) # S_{t+1} ~ p(.|S_t,A_t)
    return s_next, rng, a, reward_mean[s, a]

S_next_sym, rng_final, A_sym, R_sym = pytensor.scan(
    fn=simulate_step,
    outputs_info=[s_start_sym, rng_simulate, None, None],
    non_sequences=[pi_rollout_sym, P_sym],
    n_steps=max_steps_sym,
    return_updates=False,
)
S_sym = pt.concatenate([s_start_sym[None, :], S_next_sym[:-1]], axis=0)  # row t = S_t
simulate = pytensor.function(
    [pi_rollout_sym, s_start_sym, max_steps_sym],
    [S_sym, A_sym, R_sym],
    updates={rng_simulate: rng_final}
)

Monte Carlo with exploring starts needs every episode to begin at a chosen \((S_0, A_0)\) pair, so we draw that first transition outside the scan and hand the resulting state in as the scan’s initial value. After the forced pair the rollout is the ordinary one, so simulate_step is reused verbatim.

# exploring-starts variant: the first (state, action) pair is forced
rng_exploring_starts = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=99, name="rng_exploring_starts")
rng_after_start, s_first_sym = rng_exploring_starts.categorical(p=P_sym[s_start_sym, a_start_sym])
r_first_sym = reward_mean[s_start_sym, a_start_sym]

# after the forced first pair the rollout is the ordinary one, so `simulate_step` is reused
S_next_es_sym, rng_es_final, A_es_rest_sym, R_es_rest_sym = pytensor.scan(
    fn=simulate_step,
    outputs_info=[s_first_sym, rng_after_start, None, None],
    non_sequences=[pi_rollout_sym, P_sym],
    n_steps=max_steps_sym - 1,
    return_updates=False,
)

S_es_sym = pt.concatenate([s_start_sym[None, :], s_first_sym[None, :], S_next_es_sym[:-1]], axis=0)
A_es_sym = pt.concatenate([a_start_sym[None, :], A_es_rest_sym], axis=0)
R_es_sym = pt.concatenate([r_first_sym[None, :], R_es_rest_sym], axis=0)

simulate_exploring_starts = pytensor.function(
    [pi_rollout_sym, s_start_sym, a_start_sym, max_steps_sym],
    [S_es_sym, A_es_sym, R_es_sym],
    updates={rng_exploring_starts: rng_es_final}
)

The returns come from a second scan over the same \((T, B)\) reward block, run backwards so each \(G_t\) can reuse the \(G_{t+1}\) computed one step earlier. It is compiled once and applied to whole batches of episodes.

# discounted returns G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma * G_{t+1}, right to left
rewards_sym = pt.matrix("rewards")

def accumulate_return(r, G_next, gamma):
    """One step of the backward return recursion, G_t = R_{t+1} + gamma * G_{t+1}, for every episode.

    The scan walks the (T, B) reward block from its last row to its first, so ``G_next`` is
    the row of returns already computed for step t + 1. The return after the last step is 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    r : TensorVariable, shape (n_episodes,)
        The rewards R_{t+1}: one row of the reward block, supplied by the scan sequence.
    G_next : TensorVariable, shape (n_episodes,)
        The returns G_{t+1} from the following time step.
    gamma : TensorVariable, scalar
        Discount factor.

    Returns
    -------
    TensorVariable, shape (n_episodes,)
        The returns G_t.
    """
    return r + gamma * G_next

G_reversed = pytensor.scan(
    fn=accumulate_return,
    sequences=[rewards_sym],
    outputs_info=pt.zeros_like(rewards_sym[0]),
    non_sequences=[gamma_sym],
    go_backwards=True,
    return_updates=False,
)
returns_fn = pytensor.function([rewards_sym, gamma_sym], G_reversed[::-1])

Averaging sampled returns means summing them into buckets - one per state, or one per state-action pair - and dividing by how many landed there. inc_subtensor accumulates over repeated indices, so a single call gives both the weighted sums and the counts; the weights argument stays open for the importance-sampling ratios later on.

# scatter-add sample returns into buckets (states, or state-action pairs)
def make_aggregator(n_buckets):
    """Compile a scatter-add that sums weighted values into buckets, along with the weights.

    For every bucket j,

        sums[j] = sum over i with ids[i] = j of weights[i] * values[i],
        counts[j] = sum over i with ids[i] = j of weights[i].

    With unit weights, ``counts`` is the number of values in each bucket and ``sums / counts``
    is the sample average. With importance-sampling ratios as weights, the two are the
    numerator and denominator of the weighted importance-sampling estimate.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n_buckets : int
        Number of buckets: ``n_states`` for states, or ``n_states * n_actions`` for raveled
        state-action ids ``s * n_actions + a``.

    Returns
    -------
    callable
        Compiled PyTensor function ``(ids, values, weights) -> (sums, counts)``. ``ids`` is int64
        and ``values`` and ``weights`` are float64, all of shape (n_values,); ``sums`` and
        ``counts`` have shape (n_buckets,).
    """
    ids = pt.lvector("ids")
    values = pt.dvector("values")
    weights = pt.dvector("weights")
    sums = pt.inc_subtensor(pt.zeros((n_buckets,))[ids], weights * values)
    counts = pt.inc_subtensor(pt.zeros((n_buckets,))[ids], weights)
    return pytensor.function([ids, values, weights], [sums, counts])

aggregate_states = make_aggregator(n_states)
aggregate_state_actions = make_aggregator(n_states * n_actions)

The last ingredient separates first-visit from every-visit MC: a forward sweep through time that marks the earliest occurrence of each id within its episode. Passing this mask as the weights gives first-visit estimates; passing all ones gives every-visit.

def first_visit_mask(ids, n_buckets):
    """Flag the first occurrence of each id within its episode.

    Sweeps forward through time and marks a step True if its id has not appeared earlier in the
    same episode. Terminal steps are flagged like any other, so callers mask them out. Used as
    the weights of an aggregator, the mask gives first-visit MC; all ones gives every-visit MC.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ids : ndarray of int, shape (max_steps, n_episodes)
        The state, or the raveled state-action id ``s * n_actions + a``, at every step of every
        episode. Row t holds time step t.
    n_buckets : int
        Number of possible ids: ``n_states``, or ``n_states * n_actions``.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of bool, shape (max_steps, n_episodes)
        True where an id appears for the first time in its episode.
    """
    max_steps, n_episodes = ids.shape
    seen = np.zeros((n_episodes, n_buckets), dtype=bool)
    is_first_visit = np.zeros(ids.shape, dtype=bool)
    episodes = np.arange(n_episodes)
    for t in range(max_steps):
        is_first_visit[t] = ~seen[episodes, ids[t]]
        seen[episodes, ids[t]] = True
    return is_first_visit

title: Monte Carlo Methods
section: Sample Averages Under a Moving Policy
text:
Sample Averages Under a Moving Policy
The textbook algorithm averages all returns ever collected for each pair. But during control the policy keeps changing, so old returns are samples of the wrong (much worse) policy. Pairs that the greedy policy stops visiting only receive a thin \(\varepsilon\)-trickle of new data, and their poisoned averages can misrank actions for a very long time.
\[
\underbrace{
    \left(1 - \varepsilon + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}\right)}_{\text{greedy}
} +
\underbrace{(|\mathcal A| - 1)\cdot\tfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}}_{\text{other actions}} = 1
\]
This \(\frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal A|}\) floor on every action is exactly what makes the policy ε-soft: no action’s probability ever drops to zero, which guarantees continual exploration and lets the MC control convergence argument go through.

EPS = 0.1

def eps_greedy(Q, eps):
    """Return the ε-greedy policy of a Q table.

        pi(a|s) = 1 - eps + eps / |A|   if a = argmax_a' Q(s, a'),
                  eps / |A|             otherwise.

    Ties go to the lowest-numbered action.

    Parameters
    ----------
    Q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values.
    eps : float
        Exploration probability ε.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The policy pi(a|s). Each row sums to 1.
    """
    pi = np.full((n_states, n_actions), eps / n_actions)
    pi[np.arange(n_states), Q.argmax(axis=1)] += 1 - eps
    return pi

def sample_average_trial():
    """Run one trial of on-policy ε-greedy MC control in which Q averages every return ever seen.

    Each of 300 iterations rolls out 50 episodes, each capped at 50 steps, under the ε-greedy
    policy of the current Q (ε = ``EPS``), from start states drawn uniformly from the non-terminal
    states. Their first-visit returns are added to running sums and counts, so

        Q(s, a) = average of every first-visit return of (s, a) so far,

    including the returns collected under older, worse policies. At the end, the DP oracle
    grades the greedy policy of Q.

    Returns
    -------
    value_gap : float
        ``max_s |v_greedy(s) - v_*(s)|``, where v_greedy is the exact value of the greedy policy
        of the final Q. 0 means that policy is optimal.
    Q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The final action-value estimates.
    Q_count : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        How many returns each Q(s, a) averages.
    a_greedy : ndarray of int, shape (n_states,)
        The greedy action of the final Q in each state.
    """
    Q_sum, Q_count = np.zeros(n_states * n_actions), np.zeros(n_states * n_actions)
    Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    for iteration in range(300):
        pi_soft = eps_greedy(Q, EPS)
        s_start_iter = np_rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(~terminal), size=50).astype("int64")
        S_iter, A_iter, R_iter = simulate(pi_soft, s_start_iter, 50)
        G_iter = returns_fn(R_iter, GAMMA_GRID)
        SA_iter = S_iter * n_actions + A_iter
        first_visits_iter = first_visit_mask(SA_iter, n_states * n_actions) & ~terminal[S_iter]

        sums, counts = aggregate_state_actions(
            SA_iter[first_visits_iter].astype("int64"),
            G_iter[first_visits_iter],
            np.ones(first_visits_iter.sum())
        )

        Q_sum += sums
        Q_count += counts
        Q = np.where(Q_count > 0, Q_sum / np.maximum(Q_count, 1), 0.0).reshape(n_states, n_actions)
    a_greedy = Q.argmax(axis=1)
    pi_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    pi_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_greedy] = 1.0
    return (np.abs(evaluate_policy(pi_greedy, GAMMA_GRID) - v_star).max(), Q, Q_count.reshape(n_states, n_actions), a_greedy)

We run five trials, then open up the worst one. If its greedy policy is wrong somewhere, we print the full \(Q\) row of the offending state alongside how many returns each action was averaged from.

The rarely-explored optimal action still averages in early garbage returns at an eps-trickle of new data it would need thousands more episodes to recover. The cure is to replace the sample average with a constant step size,
\[
Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\,\big[G_t - Q(S_t, A_t)\big],
\]
an exponential recency-weighted average that forgets returns generated by long-dead policies. With forgetting, the same \(\varepsilon\)-greedy loop lands on the optimal greedy policy reliably:

ALPHA = 0.05
Q_soft = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))

soft_returns = []
for iteration in range(1000):
    pi_soft = eps_greedy(Q_soft, EPS)
    s_start_iter = np_rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(~terminal), size=50).astype("int64")
    S_iter, A_iter, R_iter = simulate(pi_soft, s_start_iter, 50)
    G_iter = returns_fn(R_iter, GAMMA_GRID)
    soft_returns.append(G_iter[0].mean())
    SA_iter = S_iter * n_actions + A_iter
    first_visits_iter = first_visit_mask(SA_iter, n_states * n_actions) & ~terminal[S_iter]

    sums, counts = aggregate_state_actions(
        SA_iter[first_visits_iter].astype("int64"),
        G_iter[first_visits_iter],
        np.ones(first_visits_iter.sum())
    )

    counts = counts.reshape(n_states, n_actions)
    batch_mean = np.where(counts > 0, sums.reshape(n_states, n_actions) / np.maximum(counts, 1), 0.0)
    alpha_effective = 1 - (1 - ALPHA) ** counts # n consecutive alpha-steps toward the batch mean
    Q_soft += alpha_effective * (batch_mean - Q_soft)

a_soft = Q_soft.argmax(axis=1)
pi_soft_greedy = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
pi_soft_greedy[np.arange(n_states), a_soft] = 1.0

An episode contributes \(\rho G \ne 0\) only if every choice was left. Any right makes \(\pi(A|S)=0\), and it also makes \(G=0\). Each visit to \(s\) continues with probability \(0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.45\), so the number of visits \(V\) is geometric, and the episode ends in the all-left-and-score way with probability \(0.05/0.55\) given it stops. Such an episode has \(G=1\) and \(\rho = 2^V\).
This implies that the expectation converges
\[
\mathbb E[\rho G] = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.45^{V-1}(0.05)\,2^V = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.1\cdot 0.9^{V-1} = 1
\]
However, the variance does not
\[
\mathbb E[(\rho G)^2] = \sum_{V\ge1} 0.2\cdot 1.8^{V-1} = \infty
\]
So the sample average keeps taking hits of size \(2^V\) and never settles. Weighted IS, in contrast, is exactly 1 here after the first matching episode because every nonzero-weight return is 1.

n_draws_sym = pt.iscalar("n_draws")
rng_infinite = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=7, name="rng_infinite")
rng_after_visits, n_visits = rng_infinite.geometric(p=0.55, size=(n_draws_sym,))
rng_infinite_final, u = rng_after_visits.uniform(size=(n_draws_sym,))
rho_times_G_draw = pt.switch(u < 0.05 / 0.55, 2.0 ** n_visits, 0.0)   # rho * G per episode
infinite_variance_draws = pytensor.function(
    [n_draws_sym],
    rho_times_G_draw,
    updates={rng_infinite: rng_infinite_final}
)

Below we run five independent runs of a million episodes each, plotted as running sample averages. The jumps are single episodes with a large \(2^V\); a curve that has just been hit looks converged for a while, until the next hit resets it.

    running_means.append(running_mean)

    annotation_position="top left"
)
inf_fig.update_layout(
    title="Ordinary Importance Sampling (IS) with infinite variance never converges",
    xaxis=dict(title="episodes (log scale)", type="log"),
    yaxis=dict(title="ordinary IS estimate"),
    template="plotly_dark",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=0.95, x=0),
)
inf_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

title: Monte Carlo Methods
text:
Incremental Implementation
Storing every return to re-average is wasteful. Sample means update incrementally, \(V_{n+1} = V_n + \frac1n (G_n - V_n)\), and weighted IS has an equally clean episode-by-episode form. With weights \(W_n = \rho_{t:T-1}\) and cumulative weight \(C_n = \sum_{k=1}^n W_k\):
\[
V_{n+1} = V_n + \frac{W_n}{C_n}\big[G_n - V_n\big], \qquad C_n = C_{n-1} + W_n .
\]
We implement the recursion as a scan over the per-episode \((G, W)\) pairs for state 6 from the previous simulation and check it reproduces the batch weighted-IS estimate exactly.

# per-episode first-visit (G, W) pairs for state 6, in episode order
visits_state6 = first_visits_is & (S_is == 6)
episode_has_state6 = visits_state6.any(axis=0)
t_first_visit = visits_state6.argmax(axis=0)[episode_has_state6]
episodes_with_state6 = np.flatnonzero(episode_has_state6)
G_state6_episodes = G_is[t_first_visit, episodes_with_state6]
W_state6_episodes = rho_is[t_first_visit, episodes_with_state6]

G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym = pt.dvector("G_episodes"), pt.dvector("W_episodes")

One step consumes an episode’s \((G, W)\), grows the cumulative weight \(C\), and moves \(V\) a fraction \(W/C\) of the way toward \(G\). Episodes whose weight is zero leave both untouched, which is what the switch guards. A scan over the sequence returns the whole trace of estimates, not just the last one.

def incremental_step(G, W, V_prev, C_prev):
    """One episode's incremental weighted-importance-sampling update of a single state's value.

        C_n = C_{n-1} + W_n,    V_{n+1} = V_n + (W_n / C_n) [ G_n - V_n ]

    While the cumulative weight is still 0 (every episode so far had weight 0), V is left
    unchanged; the switch also keeps the division safe.

    Parameters
    ----------
    G : TensorVariable, scalar
        The return G_n that follows this episode's first visit, supplied by the scan sequence.
    W : TensorVariable, scalar
        Its importance weight ``W_n = rho_{t:T-1}``, supplied by the scan sequence.
    V_prev : TensorVariable, scalar
        The estimate V_n before this episode.
    C_prev : TensorVariable, scalar
        The cumulative weight C_{n-1} before this episode.

    Returns
    -------
    V_new : TensorVariable, scalar
        The estimate V_{n+1}.
    C_new : TensorVariable, scalar
        The cumulative weight C_n.
    """
    C_new = C_prev + W
    safe_C = pt.switch(pt.gt(C_new, 0), C_new, 1.0)
    V_new = pt.switch(pt.gt(C_new, 0), V_prev + (W / safe_C) * (G - V_prev), V_prev)
    return V_new, C_new

V_trace, C_trace = pytensor.scan(
    fn=incremental_step,
    sequences=[G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym],
    outputs_info=[pt.constant(0.0, dtype="float64"), pt.constant(0.0, dtype="float64")],
    return_updates=False,
)
incremental_fn = pytensor.function([G_episodes_sym, W_episodes_sym], [V_trace, C_trace])

The incremental estimate after the last episode against the batch formula \(\sum W G / \sum W\) agree to floating-point noise because the recursion is an exact rewrite.

V_incremental, C_incremental = incremental_fn(G_state6_episodes, W_state6_episodes)
V_batch = (W_state6_episodes * G_state6_episodes).sum() / W_state6_episodes.sum()


incremental_rows = pd.DataFrame([
    dict(estimate="Incremental, final", value=V_incremental[-1]),
    dict(estimate="Batch weighted IS", value=V_batch),
    dict(estimate="Exact <i>v</i><sub>π</sub>(6)", value=v_target[6]),
])
rows_estimates = [0, 1]
row_exact = [2]

incremental_table = (
    GT(incremental_rows, rowname_col="estimate")
    .tab_header(
        title=md("**Incremental against batch weighted IS at state 6**"),
        subtitle=f"{G_state6_episodes.size:,} episodes touch state 6."
    )
    .cols_label(value=html("Estimate of <i>v</i><sub>π</sub>(6)"))
    .fmt_markdown(columns="estimate")
    .fmt_number(columns="value", rows=rows_estimates, decimals=6)
    .fmt_number(columns="value", rows=row_exact, decimals=3)
    .cols_align("right", columns="value")
)

title: Temporal-Difference Learning
text:
Utilities & Environment Setup
A hands-on companion to Chapter 6 of Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction.
The two ideas we have built so far sit at opposite ends of a spectrum:
Now we introduce a new algorithm, Temporal-difference learning, which samples one transition and bootstraps off the value of the state it lands in.
Each algorithm incrementally updates \(V(S_t)\) using a different estimate/target as shown below.
\[
V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\left[\,\text{target} - V(S_t)\right]
\]
can be given:
\[
\underbrace{G_t}_{\textbf{MC: sample, no bootstrap}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[R_{t+1} + \gamma v(S_{t+1})\mid S_t\right]}_{\textbf{DP: bootstrap, no sample}}
\qquad
\underbrace{R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1})}_{\textbf{TD(0): sample \textit{and} bootstrap}}
\]
The temporal-difference (TD) target is available one step later, making it fully incremental and online, it works on continuing (non-episodic) tasks, and it typically learns faster than Monte Carlo (MC) on the same episodes.
We will touch on the following sections:
This chapter has more running examples than any chapter so far, and each one exists to isolate a specific effect, so we build all five:
All are finite MDPs, so we can always compute the exact answer with dynamic programming and grade the learner against it.
