title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
Environments & Plotting Utilities

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytensor
import pytensor.tensor as pt
from dataclasses import dataclass, fields
import warnings
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
from great_tables import GT, loc, style, md, html

colors = px.colors.qualitative.Pastel
pio.renderers.default = "notebook_connected"
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Cannot cache compiled function")   # numba, via pytensor

print("pytensor", pytensor.__version__)

pytensor 3.0.7


As we have done before, a single Env container holds everything an algorithm could need to know about an environment. Two parts of it matter most in this chapter, because they are the two kinds of model the next section introduces:

the transition tensor \(P[s,a,s']\) - the probability of landing in \(s'\) after taking \(a\) in \(s\) - together with the reward tables is a distribution model: it lists every possible outcome with its probability;
a function that draws one next state \(S_{t+1}\sim P[s,a,\cdot]\) from those tables is a sample model: it produces one outcome at a time.

There is one change to note from the prior chapter. There, step_fn returned a single outcome for each state and action. Now it may instead return a list of (probability, s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd) outcomes, because in the stochastic windy gridworld used in the next section the same action can lead to more than one next state.

NEG_INF = -1e30 # stand-in for -inf when masking illegal actions
TIE_TOLERANCE = 1e-9 # action values this close to the best count as tied for best

@dataclass
class Env:
    name: str
    n_states: int
    n_actions: int
    P: np.ndarray              # (n_states, n_actions, n_states) transition probabilities
    reward_mean: np.ndarray    # (n_states, n_actions) expected reward
    reward_sd: np.ndarray      # (n_states, n_actions)
    terminal: np.ndarray       # (n_states,) bool
    start: np.ndarray          # (n_states,) start-state distribution
    legal_actions: np.ndarray  # (n_states, n_actions) 1.0 where the action is allowed
    reachable: np.ndarray      # (n_states,) reachable from a start state
    shape: tuple = ()          # grid shape, for printing


def make_env(name, n_states, n_actions, step_fn, terminals, starts, shape=(), legal_actions=None):
    """Build a tabular `Env` by asking a step function about every (s, a) pair.

    Terminal states absorb: every action leaves a terminal state where it is, with reward 0.
    The reachable states are found by a breadth-first search from the start states that
    follows only legal actions.

    Parameters
    ----------
    name : str
        Label for the environment. It also keys the DP oracle cache and names random generators.
    n_states, n_actions : int
        Number of states and of actions.
    step_fn : callable
        ``step_fn(s, a)`` returns ``(s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd)`` for a deterministic
        transition, or a list of ``(probability, s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd)`` outcomes
        for a stochastic one. It is never called on a terminal state.
    terminals : iterable of int
        The terminal states.
    starts : iterable of int
        The start states. Each episode starts in one of them, chosen uniformly.
    shape : tuple of int, default ()
        ``(n_rows, n_cols)`` of the grid. Used only for printing.
    legal_actions : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions), optional
        1.0 where an action is allowed, 0.0 where it is not. By default every action is legal.

    Returns
    -------
    Env
        The model ``P`` (n_states, n_actions, n_states), the reward mean and standard
        deviation (n_states, n_actions), and the terminal, start, legal-action and
        reachable arrays.
    """
    P = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states))
    reward_mean = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    reward_sd = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    terminal = np.zeros(n_states, dtype=bool); terminal[list(terminals)] = True

    for s in range(n_states):
        for a in range(n_actions):
            if terminal[s]:
                P[s, a, s] = 1.0
                continue
            outcomes = step_fn(s, a)
            if not isinstance(outcomes, list): # a single deterministic outcome
                outcomes = [(1.0, *outcomes)]
            for probability, s_next, mean, sd in outcomes:
                P[s, a, s_next] += probability
                reward_mean[s, a] += probability * mean
                reward_sd[s, a] = sd

    start = np.zeros(n_states)
    start[list(starts)] = 1.0 / len(list(starts))

    if legal_actions is None:
        legal_actions = np.ones((n_states, n_actions))

    reachable = start > 0 # Breadth-First-Search over the legal actions
    legal_P = P * (legal_actions > 0)[:, :, None]
    while True:
        frontier = legal_P[reachable & ~terminal]
        grown = reachable | (frontier.sum(axis=(0, 1)) > 0)
        if grown.sum() == reachable.sum():
            break
        reachable = grown

    return Env(name, n_states, n_actions, P, reward_mean, reward_sd, terminal, start,
               legal_actions, reachable, shape)


UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT = 0, 1, 2, 3
STEP = {UP: (0, 1), DOWN: (0, -1), LEFT: (-1, 0), RIGHT: (1, 0)} # action -> (dx, dy) when drawn

def _move(row, col, action, n_rows, n_cols):
    """Move one cell on a grid. A move off the edge leaves the agent where it is.

    Parameters
    ----------
    row, col : int
        The current cell. Row 0 is the top row.
    action : {UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT}
        The direction to move.
    n_rows, n_cols : int
        Size of the grid.

    Returns
    -------
    row, col : int
        The cell after the move.
    """
    if action == UP: row = max(row - 1, 0)
    elif action == DOWN: row = min(row + 1, n_rows - 1)
    elif action == LEFT: col = max(col - 1, 0)
    elif action == RIGHT: col = min(col + 1, n_cols - 1)
    return row, col

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class GridTheme:
    template: str    # plotly template
    background: str  # plot background, which shows in the gaps between cells
    floor: str       # fill of an open cell
    wall: str        # fill of a wall, or of a cell the agent can never reach

GRID_LIGHT = GridTheme(template="plotly_white", background="white", floor="#f2f2f2", wall="#9a9a9a")
GRID_DARK = GridTheme(template="plotly_dark", background="black", floor="#9e9d9d", wall="#4f4f4f")
GRID_GOAL = colors[4] # goal cell fill, the same in both themes
GRID_INK, GRID_ARROW = "#4a4a4a", colors[2] # labels and policy arrows, drawn on the cells in both themes

def grid_xy(s, shape):
    """Convert a state id to (x, y) plot coordinates, with grid row 0 drawn at the top.

    Parameters
    ----------
    s : int
        The state, numbered ``row * n_cols + col``.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The grid's (n_rows, n_cols).

    Returns
    -------
    x, y : int
        The column, and the row counted up from the bottom.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    row, col = divmod(int(s), n_cols)
    return col, n_rows - 1 - row

def grid_panels(panel_titles, shape, title="", n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=34, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Make an empty figure with one subplot per panel, each holding a grid of square cells.

    The figure is sized so that every cell is ``cell_px`` pixels wide, and the panels are laid out
    left to right, then top to bottom.

    Parameters
    ----------
    panel_titles : list of str
        One title per panel.
    shape : tuple of (int, int)
        The (n_rows, n_cols) of the grid. Every panel shares it.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title. Plotly HTML (<b>, <br>, <sup>) works.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 34
        Width of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The plotly template and plot background. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        The figure, with the axes of every panel hidden and scaled so the cells are square.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = shape
    n_panels = len(panel_titles)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or n_panels
    n_panel_rows = -(-n_panels // n_panel_cols) # ceiling division
    gap_x_px, gap_y_px = 20, 40 # between panels
    plot_width = n_panel_cols * n_cols * cell_px + (n_panel_cols - 1) * gap_x_px
    plot_height = n_panel_rows * n_rows * cell_px + (n_panel_rows - 1) * gap_y_px

    fig = make_subplots(
        rows=n_panel_rows,
        cols=n_panel_cols,
        subplot_titles=[f"<b>{t}</b>" for t in panel_titles],
        horizontal_spacing=gap_x_px / plot_width,
        vertical_spacing=gap_y_px / plot_height
    )

    for row in range(1, n_panel_rows + 1):
        for col in range(1, n_panel_cols + 1):
            x_axis = fig.get_subplot(row, col).xaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
            fig.update_xaxes(range=[-0.55, n_cols - 0.45], visible=False, row=row, col=col)
            fig.update_yaxes(range=[-0.55, n_rows - 0.45], visible=False, row=row, col=col)

    margin = dict(l=10, r=10, b=10, t=(80 if title else 0) + 30)
    fig.update_layout(
        title=title,
        margin=margin,
        template=theme.template,
        plot_bgcolor=theme.background,
        showlegend=False
    )
    return fig

def draw_cells(fig, env, fills, labels, row=1, col=1, pad=0.04, label_offset=0.0):
    """Draw one filled square per state into a subplot, with an optional label on top.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fig : plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        A figure from `grid_panels`. It is changed in place.
    env : Env
        Supplies the grid shape.
    fills : list of str, length n_states
        The fill color of each state's cell.
    labels : dict of {int: str}
        Text drawn in the middle of a cell, by state, e.g. ``{start: "S"}``.
    row, col : int, default 1, 1
        The panel to draw into.
    pad : float, default 0.04
        Gap around each cell, in cell widths.
    label_offset : float, default 0.0
        How far to move the labels up, in cell heights. -0.3 puts them under an arrow.
    """
    for s in range(env.n_states):
        x, y = grid_xy(s, env.shape)
        fig.add_shape(
            type="rect",
            x0=x - 0.5 + pad,
            x1=x + 0.5 - pad,
            y0=y - 0.5 + pad,
            y1=y + 0.5 - pad,
            fillcolor=fills[s],
            line_width=0,
            layer="below",
            row=row, col=col
        )
    for s, label in labels.items():
        x, y = grid_xy(s, env.shape)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x, y=y + label_offset, text=f"<b>{label}</b>", showarrow=False,
                           font=dict(size=14, color=GRID_INK), row=row, col=col)

def draw_arrows(fig, env, actions, states, row=1, col=1, color=GRID_ARROW):
    """Draw an arrow in each of the given states, pointing the way its action moves.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fig : plotly.graph_objects.Figure
        A figure from `grid_panels`. It is changed in place.
    env : Env
        Supplies the grid shape.
    actions : array_like of int, shape (n_states,)
        The action in each state. Only the entries for ``states`` are drawn.
    states : array_like of int
        The states that get an arrow.
    row, col : int, default 1, 1
        The panel to draw into.
    color : str, default GRID_ARROW
        The arrow color.
    """
    subplot = fig.get_subplot(row, col)
    x_ref = subplot.xaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
    y_ref = subplot.yaxis.plotly_name.replace("axis", "")
    for s in states:
        x, y = grid_xy(s, env.shape)
        dx, dy = STEP[int(actions[s])]
        fig.add_annotation(
            x=x + 0.34 * dx,
            y=y + 0.34 * dy,
            ax=x - 0.22 * dx,
            ay=y - 0.22 * dy,
            xref=x_ref, yref=y_ref,
            axref=x_ref, ayref=y_ref,
            showarrow=True,
            arrowhead=2, arrowsize=1.0, arrowwidth=2.2, arrowcolor=color
        )

def values_figure(values, env, title="", fmt=".1f", n_panel_cols=None, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Draw one number per state, laid out as the grid and colored by size.

    Each panel has its own color scale, so the colors compare states within a panel; the printed
    numbers carry the values. Unreachable states are left blank.

    Parameters
    ----------
    values : dict of {str: array_like of shape (n_states,)}
        One panel per entry: its title, and the number for each state (e.g. a state-value
        function).
    env : Env
        Supplies the grid shape and the reachable states.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title.
    fmt : str, default ".1f"
        d3 format spec for the numbers printed in the cells.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The plotly template and plot background. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = env.shape
    fig = grid_panels(list(values), env.shape, title, n_panel_cols, cell_px=46, theme=theme)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or len(values)
    for i, v in enumerate(values.values()):
        grid = np.where(env.reachable, np.asarray(v, dtype=float), np.nan).reshape(n_rows, n_cols)
        state = np.arange(env.n_states).reshape(n_rows, n_cols)
        fig.add_heatmap(
            x=np.arange(n_cols),
            y=np.arange(n_rows),
            z=grid[::-1], # grid row 0 at the top
            customdata=state[::-1],
            colorscale="Teal",
            showscale=False,
            texttemplate=f"%{{z:{fmt}}}",
            xgap=3,
            ygap=3,
            hovertemplate=f"state %{{customdata}}: <b>%{{z:{fmt}}}</b><extra></extra>",
            row=i // n_panel_cols + 1, col=i % n_panel_cols + 1
        )
    return fig

def policy_figure(policies, env, title="", extra=None, n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=34, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Draw one arrow per state for each deterministic policy, laid out as the grid.

    Unreachable states are grey and terminal states are the goal color, labeled "G". A state in
    ``extra`` shows its label instead of an arrow.

    Parameters
    ----------
    policies : dict of {str: array_like of int, shape (n_states,)}
        One panel per entry: its title, and the action taken in each state.
    env : Env
        Supplies the grid shape and the terminal and reachable states.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title.
    extra : dict of {int: str}, optional
        Labels drawn in place of the arrows, by state, e.g. ``{start: "S"}``.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 34
        Width of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The template, background and floor and wall fills. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
    """
    extra = extra or {}
    fills = [
        theme.wall if not env.reachable[s] else GRID_GOAL if env.terminal[s] else theme.floor
        for s in range(env.n_states)
    ]
    labels = {**{int(s): "G" for s in np.flatnonzero(env.terminal)}, **extra}
    has_arrow = env.reachable & ~env.terminal
    has_arrow[list(extra)] = False
    fig = grid_panels(list(policies), env.shape, title, n_panel_cols, cell_px, theme)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or len(policies)
    for i, actions in enumerate(policies.values()):
        row, col = i // n_panel_cols + 1, i % n_panel_cols + 1
        draw_cells(fig, env, fills, labels, row, col)
        draw_arrows(fig, env, actions, np.flatnonzero(has_arrow), row, col)
    return fig

def maze_figure(mazes, title="", n_panel_cols=None, cell_px=34, theme=GRID_LIGHT):
    """Draw mazes: grey walls, a lighter floor, "S" at the start and the goal colored and labeled "G".

    Parameters
    ----------
    mazes : dict of {str: Env}
        One panel per entry: its title, and the maze. Walls are a maze's unreachable states.
        Every maze must have the same grid shape.
    title : str, default ""
        The figure title.
    n_panel_cols : int, optional
        Panels per row of the figure. The default puts every panel in one row.
    cell_px : int, default 34
        Width of one grid cell, in pixels.
    theme : GridTheme, default GRID_LIGHT
        The template, background and floor and wall fills. GRID_DARK for the book's dark theme.

    Returns
    -------
    plotly.graph_objects.Figure
    """
    shape = next(iter(mazes.values())).shape
    fig = grid_panels(list(mazes), shape, title, n_panel_cols, cell_px, theme)
    n_panel_cols = n_panel_cols or len(mazes)
    for i, env in enumerate(mazes.values()):
        fills = [
            theme.wall if not env.reachable[s] else GRID_GOAL if env.terminal[s] else theme.floor
            for s in range(env.n_states)
        ]
        labels = {int(np.argmax(env.start)): "S", **{int(s): "G" for s in np.flatnonzero(env.terminal)}}
        draw_cells(fig, env, fills, labels, row=i // n_panel_cols + 1, col=i % n_panel_cols + 1)
    return fig

These are the environments. Each section explains why it uses the one it does.

dyna_maze: A \(6\times9\) maze with seven wall cells, a start \(S\) on the left and a goal \(G\) in the top-right corner. Every reward is \(0\) except \(+1\) for reaching \(G\). With \(\gamma = 0.95\) a reward that arrives later is worth less, and that discount is the only thing that makes a short path better than a long one. The shortest path takes 14 steps.
blocking_maze / shortcut_maze: The same \(6\times9\) board, with a wall across row 3 that has a single gap in it. Each maze comes in a before and an after version that differ only in where the gap is. Both versions number their states the same way, so an agent can carry its \(Q\) table and its model straight across the change. Like a real agent, it is never told that the maze changed.
stochastic_windy: Windy gridworld, except that in a windy column the wind is random: the column’s usual strength, one more, or one less, a third of the time each. It is the one board where a sample model and a distribution model really differ, because a single action can lead to up to three different next states.
cliff: The cliff environment we have seen in the previous chapters.

Two more environments are built later, inside their own sections: the random tasks of Trajectory Sampling and the racetrack of RTDP. They are too large to store as a dense \(P\) tensor.

def maze_env(name, walls, start, goal, n_rows=6, n_cols=9, goal_reward=1.0):
    """Build a deterministic maze.

    Moving into a wall or off the board leaves the agent where it is. Every reward is 0
    except ``goal_reward`` for the step into the goal, and rewards have no noise.

    Parameters
    ----------
    name : str
        Label for the environment.
    walls : set of (int, int)
        The ``(row, col)`` cells the agent cannot enter.
    start, goal : (int, int)
        The ``(row, col)`` cells of the start state and of the single terminal state.
    n_rows, n_cols : int, default 6, 9
        Size of the grid.
    goal_reward : float, default 1.0
        Reward for the step into the goal.

    Returns
    -------
    Env
        The maze, with 4 actions (UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT).
    """
    start_state = start[0] * n_cols + start[1]
    goal_state = goal[0] * n_cols + goal[1]
    def step(s, a):
        "the step_fn for make_env: (s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd) of one move"
        row, col = divmod(s, n_cols)
        row_next, col_next = _move(row, col, a, n_rows, n_cols)
        if (row_next, col_next) in walls:
            row_next, col_next = row, col
        s_next = row_next * n_cols + col_next
        reward = goal_reward if s_next == goal_state else 0.0
        return s_next, reward, 0.0 # (s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd = 0: no noise)
    return make_env(name, n_rows * n_cols, 4, step, [goal_state], [start_state], shape=(n_rows, n_cols))

DYNA_WALLS = {(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 5), (0, 7), (1, 7), (2, 7)}
dyna_maze = maze_env("dyna_maze", DYNA_WALLS, start=(2, 0), goal=(0, 8))

def wall_across_row_3(columns):
    """Return the wall cells ``(3, col)`` for each col in `columns`, for the changing mazes."""
    return {(3, col) for col in columns}

blocking_before = maze_env("blocking_before", wall_across_row_3(range(0, 8)), start=(5, 3), goal=(0, 8))
blocking_after = maze_env("blocking_after", wall_across_row_3(range(1, 9)), start=(5, 3), goal=(0, 8))
shortcut_before = maze_env("shortcut_before", wall_across_row_3(range(1, 9)), start=(5, 3), goal=(0, 8))
shortcut_after = maze_env("shortcut_after", wall_across_row_3(range(1, 8)), start=(5, 3), goal=(0, 8))
changing_mazes = (blocking_before, blocking_after, shortcut_before, shortcut_after)


maze_figure({"dyna_maze": dyna_maze}).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))
maze_figure(
    {env.name: env for env in changing_mazes},
    title="<b>Mazes that change partway through</b>",
    n_panel_cols=2
).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            


                            
                                            



maze_figure({"dyna_maze": dyna_maze}, theme=GRID_DARK).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))
maze_figure(
    {env.name: env for env in changing_mazes},
    title="<b>Mazes that change partway through</b>",
    n_panel_cols=2,
    theme=GRID_DARK
).show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            


                            
                                            



WIND = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0])

def stochastic_windy_env(n_rows=7, n_cols=10, step_reward=-1.0):
    """Build the stochastic windy gridworld.

    The wind pushes the agent up after each move. In a column with any wind, the push is
    the column's mean wind (``WIND[col]``), one more, or one less, each a third of the time.
    So an action has up to three possible next states. Every step earns ``step_reward``,
    without noise, so with no discounting -v(s) is the expected number of steps to the goal.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n_rows, n_cols : int, default 7, 10
        Size of the grid.
    step_reward : float, default -1.0
        Reward on every step.

    Returns
    -------
    Env
        The gridworld, with 4 actions, start at (3, 0) and goal at (3, 7).
    """
    def step(s, a):
        "the step_fn for make_env: one outcome without wind, three equally likely ones with it"
        row, col = divmod(s, n_cols)
        row_next, col_next = _move(row, col, a, n_rows, n_cols)
        wind = WIND[col]

        def blown(push):
            "the state after the wind pushes the agent up `push` rows from where it moved to"
            return np.clip(row_next - push, 0, n_rows - 1) * n_cols + col_next

        if wind == 0:
            return blown(0), step_reward, 0.0 # (s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd = 0: no noise)
        return [(1 / 3, blown(push), step_reward, 0.0) for push in (wind - 1, wind, wind + 1)]
    return make_env("stochastic_windy", n_rows * n_cols, 4, step, [3 * n_cols + 7], [3 * n_cols],
                    shape=(n_rows, n_cols))

def cliff_env(n_rows=4, n_cols=12, step_reward=-1.0, cliff_reward=-100.0):
    """Build the cliff-walking gridworld.

    The start and the goal are the two bottom corners, and the cells between them are the
    cliff. Stepping into the cliff earns ``cliff_reward`` and sends the agent back to the
    start. Every other step earns ``step_reward``. Rewards have no noise.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n_rows, n_cols : int, default 4, 12
        Size of the grid.
    step_reward : float, default -1.0
        Reward for a step that does not enter the cliff.
    cliff_reward : float, default -100.0
        Reward for stepping into the cliff.

    Returns
    -------
    Env
        The gridworld, with 4 actions.
    """
    start_state = (n_rows - 1) * n_cols
    goal = (n_rows - 1) * n_cols + n_cols - 1
    cliff_cells = {(n_rows - 1) * n_cols + col for col in range(1, n_cols - 1)}
    def step(s, a):
        "the step_fn for make_env: (s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd) of one move"
        row, col = _move(*divmod(s, n_cols), a, n_rows, n_cols)
        s_next = row * n_cols + col
        if s_next in cliff_cells:
            return start_state, cliff_reward, 0.0 # (s_next, reward_mean, reward_sd = 0: no noise)
        return s_next, step_reward, 0.0
    return make_env("cliff", n_rows * n_cols, 4, step, [goal], [start_state],
                    shape=(n_rows, n_cols))

windy = stochastic_windy_env()
cliff = cliff_env()

text:
The DP oracle
The same oracle we have been using in previous chapters that has the following three parts:

iterative policy evaluation, which computes \(v_\pi\), the value of following a given policy \(\pi\)
value iteration, which computes \(v_*\), the value of acting optimally
the one-step lookahead \(q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}P[s,a,s']\,v(s')\), which turns state values into action values: the expected reward for taking \(a\), plus the discounted value of wherever \(a\) leads.







Note



This chapter uses more environments than the last one, and some of them are needed for only a single experiment. So rather than compiling the oracle for every environment up front, exact compiles it the first time an environment asks for it, and reuses it after that.



def make_dp(env, n_iters=2000):
    """Compile exact dynamic programming for one environment: the "DP oracle".

    Both solvers start from v = 0 and apply ``n_iters`` synchronous sweeps, with terminal
    states held at 0. Policy evaluation applies the Bellman expectation backup,

        v(s) <- sum_a pi(a|s) [ r(s, a) + gamma * sum_s' p(s'|s, a) v(s') ],

    and value iteration applies the Bellman optimality backup, a max over the legal actions
    in place of the sum over pi.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        Supplies the model: ``P``, ``reward_mean``, ``terminal`` and ``legal_actions``.
    n_iters : int, default 2000
        Number of sweeps for each solver.

    Returns
    -------
    evaluate_policy : callable
        ``evaluate_policy(pi, gamma) -> v_pi``, with ``pi`` of shape (n_states, n_actions)
        and ``v_pi`` of shape (n_states,).
    optimal_values : callable
        ``optimal_values(gamma) -> v_*``, shape (n_states,).
    action_values_of : callable
        ``action_values_of(v, gamma) -> q``, the one-step lookahead
        ``q(s, a) = r(s, a) + gamma * sum_s' p(s'|s, a) v(s')``, shape (n_states, n_actions).
    """
    P = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.P)
    reward = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_mean)
    not_terminal = pt.as_tensor_variable((~env.terminal).astype("float64"))
    legal_actions = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    gamma = pt.scalar("gamma")
    pi = pt.matrix("pi")
    v_in = pt.vector("v")

    def q_from(v, gamma):
        "q(s, a) = r(s, a) + gamma * sum_s' p(s'|s, a) v(s'), for every (s, a)"
        return reward + gamma * (P * v[None, None, :]).sum(axis=2)

    def expectation_step(v, pi, gamma):
        "one sweep of policy evaluation: v_{k+1}(s) = sum_a pi(a|s) q_k(s, a); terminals stay 0"
        return not_terminal * (pi * q_from(v, gamma)).sum(axis=1)

    def optimality_step(v, gamma):
        "one sweep of value iteration: v_{k+1}(s) = max over the legal a of q_k(s, a); terminals stay 0"
        q =pt.where(legal_actions > 0, q_from(v, gamma), NEG_INF)
        return not_terminal * q.max(axis=1)

    v_eval = pytensor.scan(
        fn=expectation_step,
        outputs_info=pt.zeros((env.n_states,)),
        non_sequences=[pi, gamma],
        n_steps=n_iters,
        return_updates=False
    )

    v_star = pytensor.scan(
        fn=optimality_step,
        outputs_info=pt.zeros((env.n_states,)),
        non_sequences=[gamma],
        n_steps=n_iters,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return (pytensor.function([pi, gamma], v_eval[-1]), # evaluate_policy
            pytensor.function([gamma], v_star[-1]), # optimal_values
            pytensor.function([v_in, gamma], q_from(v_in, gamma))) # action_values_of


ORACLE = {}

def exact(env, gamma, pi=None):
    """Return the exact state and action values from the DP oracle.

    The oracle for each environment is compiled on first use and cached in ``ORACLE``
    under ``env.name``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The environment.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.
    pi : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions), optional
        A policy, as pi(a|s). If given, return v_pi and q_pi; otherwise v_* and q_*.

    Returns
    -------
    v : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        v_pi or v_*.
    q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The matching action values, ``r(s, a) + gamma * sum_s' p(s'|s, a) v(s')``, set to 0
        in terminal states.
    """
    if env.name not in ORACLE:
        ORACLE[env.name] = make_dp(env)
    evaluate_policy, optimal_values, action_values_of = ORACLE[env.name]
    v = evaluate_policy(pi, gamma) if pi is not None else optimal_values(gamma)
    q = action_values_of(v, gamma)
    q[env.terminal] = 0.0
    return v, q

def greedy_pi(Q, env):
    """Return the deterministic greedy policy of Q, as a table pi(a|s).

    Ties go to the lowest-numbered legal action (``argmax`` order). Use `greedy_ties_split`
    to split them instead.

    Parameters
    ----------
    Q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values.
    env : Env
        Supplies the legal actions.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        1.0 on the greedy legal action of each state, 0.0 elsewhere.
    """
    pi = np.zeros((env.n_states, env.n_actions))
    pi[np.arange(env.n_states),
       np.where(env.legal_actions > 0, Q, NEG_INF).argmax(axis=1)] = 1.0
    return pi

GAMMA_MAZE = 0.95
GAMMA_WINDY = 1.0 # the windy gridworld is undiscounted
v_star_maze, q_star_maze = exact(dyna_maze, GAMMA_MAZE)
start_maze = int(np.argmax(dyna_maze.start))
shortest_maze = int(round(1 + np.log(v_star_maze[start_maze]) / np.log(GAMMA_MAZE)))
v_star_windy, q_star_windy = exact(windy, GAMMA_WINDY)

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
Q-planning as a scan
The whole planner is a scan over planning updates, with many independent runs computed side by side. We build it in two versions, which differ only in how step 2 uses the model:

The sample version asks the sample model for one next state and reward, exactly as written above
The expected version uses the distribution model instead. Rather than one sampled next state, it averages over all of them, weighted by their probabilities: \(Q(S,A) \leftarrow \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid S,A)\left[r(S,A) + \gamma\max_a Q(s',a)\right]\). This is called an expected update. It amounts to value iteration on \(Q\), applied to one randomly chosen pair at a time.

Only the lines that leverage the model differ. The point being that planning loop is identical, and the kind of model decides what each update can use.
The outer scan saves a copy of \(Q\) at evenly spaced checkpoints, so that we can track the error as planning goes on. The inner scan does the updates between checkpoints.

def make_q_planning(env, update, seed):
    """Build a compiled random-sample one-step tabular Q-planning function.

    Each planning step picks a state-action pair uniformly from the plannable pairs (legal actions
    in reachable, non-terminal states), queries the model, and applies a one-step Q-learning update
    to the simulated transition. Many independent runs are planned in parallel.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        Tabular environment exposing the model: ``P`` (n_states, n_actions, n_states) transition
        probabilities, ``reward_mean`` and ``reward_sd`` (n_states, n_actions), boolean ``terminal``
        and ``reachable`` (n_states,), ``legal_actions`` (n_states, n_actions) mask, ``n_actions``
        and ``name``.
    update : {'sample', 'expected'}
        - ``'sample'`` draws one (R, S') from the sample model and applies a Q-learning update.
        - ``'expected'`` uses the distribution model, summing over every successor weighted by its
           probability and using the mean reward.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    f : pytensor.compile.executor.Function
        Compiled PyTensor function with inputs
        ``(Q_init, alpha, gamma, n_checkpoints, updates_per_checkpoint)`` and output ``Q``.

        - ``Q_init``: ndarray, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions) -- initial action values.
        - ``alpha``: ndarray, shape (n_runs,) -- step size for each run.
        - ``gamma``: float -- discount factor.
        - ``n_checkpoints``: int -- number of times Q is recorded.
        - ``updates_per_checkpoint``: int -- planning updates between checkpoints.

        ``Q`` has shape (n_checkpoints, n_runs, n_states, n_actions): the action values after
        each checkpoint (``Q_init`` itself is not included). The random generator state carries
        over between calls.
    """
    P = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.P)
    reward_mean = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_mean)
    reward_sd = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_sd)
    not_terminal = pt.as_tensor_variable((~env.terminal).astype("float64"))
    legal_actions = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    plannable = (env.legal_actions > 0) & (env.reachable & ~env.terminal)[:, None]
    pair_distribution = pt.as_tensor_variable((plannable / plannable.sum()).reshape(-1))
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name=f"rng_qplan_{update}_{env.name}")

    Q_init = pt.dtensor3("Q0")
    alpha = pt.dvector("alpha")
    gamma = pt.scalar("gamma")
    n_checkpoints = pt.iscalar("n_checkpoints")
    updates_per_checkpoint = pt.iscalar("k")

    def best_value(Q):
        "max_a Q(s, a) over the legal actions, for every state -> (n_runs, n_states)"
        return pt.where(legal_actions[None] > 0, Q, NEG_INF).max(axis=2)

    def q_planning_step(rng, Q, alpha, gamma):
        """One planning update in every run: Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha * (target - Q(s, a)).

        With sample updates, ``target = R + gamma * max_a' Q(S', a')`` for one (R, S') drawn
        from the model. With expected updates,
        ``target = r(s, a) + gamma * sum_s' p(s'|s, a) max_a' Q(s', a')``.
        The max is 0 when S' is terminal.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        Q : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values before the update.
        alpha : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            Step size of each run.
        gamma : TensorVariable, scalar
            Discount factor.

        Returns
        -------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The advanced generator.
        Q : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values after the update. Only one (s, a) per run changes.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        # 1. a state and action at random
        rng, pair = rng.categorical(p=pt.ones((Q.shape[0], 1)) * pair_distribution[None, :])
        s, a = pair // env.n_actions, pair % env.n_actions

        if update == "sample":
            # 2. the sample model: one next state and reward
            rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a])
            rng, r = rng.normal(loc=reward_mean[s, a], scale=reward_sd[s, a])
            target = r + gamma * not_terminal[s_next] * best_value(Q)[runs, s_next]
        else:
            # 2. the distribution model: every next state, weighted by its probability
            target = reward_mean[s, a] + gamma * (P[s, a] * not_terminal * best_value(Q)).sum(axis=1)
        # 3. one-step tabular Q-learning on the simulated transition
        return rng, pt.inc_subtensor(Q[runs, s, a], alpha * (target - Q[runs, s, a]))

    def checkpoint(rng, Q, alpha, gamma, k):
        "k planning updates in a row; return only the last Q"
        rng, Q_seq = pytensor.scan(
            fn=q_planning_step,
            outputs_info=[rng, Q],
            non_sequences=[alpha, gamma],
            n_steps=k,
            return_updates=False
        )
        return rng, Q_seq[-1]

    rng_final, Q_out = pytensor.scan(
        fn=checkpoint,
        outputs_info=[rng_shared, Q_init],
        non_sequences=[alpha, gamma, updates_per_checkpoint],
        n_steps=n_checkpoints,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return pytensor.function(
        [Q_init, alpha, gamma, n_checkpoints, updates_per_checkpoint],
        Q_out,
        updates={rng_shared: rng_final}
    )

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
Stochastic Windy Gridworld
We plan on the stochastic windy gridworld, with no discounting (\(\gamma = 1\)). Each planner gets twenty independent runs, starts from \(Q = 0\), and makes 100,000 planning updates. No real episodes are run at all: every transition comes directly from the model. The sample planner is run with two constant step sizes, \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(\alpha = 0.3\). The expected planner uses \(\alpha = 1\). It has no sampling noise, so there is nothing for a smaller step to average away, and it can jump straight to its target.
The oracle grades each planner in two ways:

The RMSE of \(Q\) against \(q_*\), over the 276 state-action pairs a planner can pick, measures how accurate the values are.
The fraction of states whose greedy action is optimal: states where the action with the highest \(Q\) is also a best action under \(q_*\), that is, \(q_*(s, \arg\max_a Q(s,a)) = v_*(s)\) - measures whether the policy those values imply is correct.

These two metrics can tell very different stories. To pick the right action, the values only have to be in the right order, so the policy can be right long before the values are accurate.

N_RUNS_QPLAN = 20
N_CHECKPOINTS_QPLAN, UPDATES_PER_CHECKPOINT_QPLAN = 40, 2500
plannable_windy = (windy.legal_actions > 0) & (windy.reachable & ~windy.terminal)[:, None]
live_windy = windy.reachable & ~windy.terminal
Q_init_qplan = np.zeros((N_RUNS_QPLAN, windy.n_states, windy.n_actions))

planners_qplan = {  # label -> (update, alpha)
    "sample, alpha = 0.1": ("sample", 0.1),
    "sample, alpha = 0.3": ("sample", 0.3),
    "expected, alpha = 1": ("expected", 1.0),
}

def greedy_is_optimal(Q, env, q_star, v_star):
    """Return the fraction of live states whose greedy action is an optimal one.

    A live state is reachable and not terminal. The greedy action of Q is optimal when
    ``q_*(s, greedy) >= v_*(s) - TIE_TOLERANCE``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    Q : ndarray, shape (..., n_states, n_actions)
        Action values, with any leading batch axes (e.g. checkpoints and runs).
    env : Env
        Supplies the legal actions and the live states.
    q_star : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Optimal action values.
    v_star : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        Optimal state values.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (...)
        The fraction, for each entry of the leading axes of Q.
    """
    live = env.reachable & ~env.terminal
    greedy = np.where(env.legal_actions > 0, Q, NEG_INF).argmax(axis=-1) # (..., n_states)
    chosen = np.take_along_axis(np.broadcast_to(q_star, Q.shape), greedy[..., None], axis=-1)[..., 0]
    return (chosen >= v_star - TIE_TOLERANCE)[..., live].mean(axis=-1)


rmse_qplan, optimal_qplan = {}, {}
for label, (update, alpha) in planners_qplan.items():
    planner = make_q_planning(windy, update, seed=11)
    Q_seq = planner(
        Q_init_qplan,
        np.full(N_RUNS_QPLAN, alpha),
        GAMMA_WINDY,
        N_CHECKPOINTS_QPLAN,
        UPDATES_PER_CHECKPOINT_QPLAN
    )

    Q_seq = np.concatenate([Q_init_qplan[None], Q_seq]) # prepend the zero table
    errors = (Q_seq - q_star_windy)[:, :, plannable_windy]
    rmse_qplan[label] = np.sqrt((errors ** 2).mean(axis=2)).mean(axis=1)
    optimal_qplan[label] = greedy_is_optimal(Q_seq, windy, q_star_windy, v_star_windy).mean(axis=1)

updates_qplan = np.arange(N_CHECKPOINTS_QPLAN + 1) * UPDATES_PER_CHECKPOINT_QPLAN


qplan_fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1,
    cols=2,
    subplot_titles=(r"$\text{RMSE of Q against }q_*$", r"$\text{states whose greedy action is optimal}$")
)

for i, label in enumerate(planners_qplan):
    dash = "dot" if label.startswith("expected") else "solid"

    qplan_fig.add_scatter(
        x=updates_qplan,
        y=rmse_qplan[label],
        mode="lines",
        name=label,
        legendgroup=label,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5, dash=dash),
        hovertemplate="<b>Updates</b>: %{x}<br><b>RMSE</b>: %{y:.3f}",
        row=1, col=1
    )

    qplan_fig.add_scatter(
        x=updates_qplan,
        y=optimal_qplan[label],
        mode="lines",
        name=label,
        legendgroup=label,
        showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5, dash=dash),
        hovertemplate="<b>Updates</b>: %{x}<br><b>Fraction of States</b>: %{y:.1%}",
        row=1, col=2
    )

qplan_fig.update_xaxes(title_text="planning updates")
qplan_fig.update_yaxes(
    title_text="RMSE (log scale)",
    type="log",
    range=[-3, 1.5],
    row=1,
    col=1
)
qplan_fig.update_yaxes(title_text="fraction of states", tickformat=".0%", row=1, col=2)

qplan_fig.update_layout(
    title="<b>Random-sample one-step Q-planning</b> on the stochastic windy gridworld"
          f"<br><sup>{N_RUNS_QPLAN} runs per curve, no real episodes run</sup>",
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.18, x=0),
    margin=dict(t=100, b=100)
)

qplan_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            



qplan_fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1,
    cols=2,
    subplot_titles=(r"$\text{RMSE of Q against }q_*$", r"$\text{states whose greedy action is optimal}$")
)

for i, label in enumerate(planners_qplan):
    dash = "dot" if label.startswith("expected") else "solid"

    qplan_fig.add_scatter(
        x=updates_qplan,
        y=rmse_qplan[label],
        mode="lines",
        name=label,
        legendgroup=label,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5, dash=dash),
        hovertemplate="<b>Updates</b>: %{x}<br><b>RMSE</b>: %{y:.3f}",
        row=1, col=1
    )

    qplan_fig.add_scatter(
        x=updates_qplan,
        y=optimal_qplan[label],
        mode="lines",
        name=label,
        legendgroup=label,
        showlegend=False,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5, dash=dash),
        hovertemplate="<b>Updates</b>: %{x}<br><b>Fraction of States</b>: %{y:.1%}",
        row=1, col=2
    )

qplan_fig.update_xaxes(title_text="planning updates")
qplan_fig.update_yaxes(
    title_text="RMSE (log scale)",
    type="log",
    range=[-3, 1.5],
    row=1,
    col=1
)
qplan_fig.update_yaxes(title_text="fraction of states", tickformat=".0%", row=1, col=2)

qplan_fig.update_layout(
    title="<b>Random-sample one-step Q-planning</b> on the stochastic windy gridworld"
          f"<br><sup>{N_RUNS_QPLAN} runs per curve, no real episodes run</sup>",
    template="plotly_dark",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.18, x=0),
    margin=dict(t=100, b=100)
)

qplan_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            


Not a single real episode was run! Every transition came out of the model and all three planners move toward \(q_*\).

The expected planner is exact, and fast. Its RMSE is \(0.004\) after 25,000 updates and zero by 50,000. From 20,000 updates on, every greedy action is optimal. It is value iteration on \(Q\), one random pair at a time, so it converges to the same answer as Chapter 4’s value iteration. That accuracy has a price, though: in a windy column each expected update had to look up \(\max_a Q(s',a)\) for three possible next states, where a sample update looks up only one.
The sample planner gets close and then stalls, and \(\alpha\) decides how close. With \(\alpha = 0.3\) the error falls quickly and then stops improving around \(1.35\). With \(\alpha = 0.1\) it is much slower at first but ends lower: \(0.76\) at 100,000, and still falling. The reason is because of the noise in the samples. Each update moves \(Q\) a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way toward whatever gust of wind was just sampled, so with a constant step size the estimate keeps jumping around the true value and never settles. It ends up fluctuating in a noise band around \(q_*\), and a larger \(\alpha\) means a wider band. This is the same plateau we saw with constant-\(\alpha\) Temporal Difference.
The policy is right long before the values are. After 100,000 updates, the \(\alpha = 0.1\) planner’s values are still off by \(0.76\) on average, but 96% of states already have an optimal greedy action. The noise only flips the choice of action where it is larger than the gap between the best action and the second best.

The book notes that this kind of planning is incremental. Each update is small and self-contained, so planning can be stopped, resumed, or pointed somewhere else at any moment. Which is what we would want to do if the agent is going to plan in the gaps between real actions.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
section: Dyna as a scan over time steps
text:
Dyna as a scan over time steps
The previous chapters used two nested scans: an outer one over episodes, and an inner one over a fixed max_steps time steps within each episode. An episode that finished early was padded out to max_steps with steps that did nothing. For plain Q-learning that padding is inconsequential. For Dyna it would be very expensive, because every padded step would still run \(n\) planning updates.
So this learner is a single flat scan over time steps. When an episode ends, the agent is put back at the start within that same step and simply carries on. Each step also outputs a done flag, and afterwards we use those flags to cut the long stream of steps back into episodes.
The scan carries the agent’s internal state from one step to the next, for all runs at once. That includes the current position, \(Q\) table, and model. The model consists of three tables:

model_next[s, a]: the next state seen after taking \(a\) in \(s\)
model_reward[s, a]: the reward seen
tried[s, a]: 1 once \((s, a)\) has actually been taken in the real environment.

Planning is a second scan, nested inside each time step. The pseudocode’s two random choices become two categorical draws: “a random previously observed state” is drawn from the states that have at least one tried action, and “a random action previously taken in \(S\)” is drawn from that state’s row of tried.
In the following sections we add two variants, Dyna-Q+ and prioritized sweeping, which change only the planning step. So all three planners are built by one function, make_dyna, in the same way that the previous chapter kept all of its returns in one function.
We need to talk about how we will be handling ties, because it is very important. \(Q\) starts at zero, so until the agent first reaches the goal, every action in each state has the same value. Acting greedily means taking an argmax, and argmax breaks ties by picking the first action; in our case action 0, “up”. The result would be an agent that always tries to go up first, which is not how the book’s agent behaves. The book breaks ties at random, so eps_greedy_probs allocates the greedy probability evenly between all the actions tied for best.

def eps_greedy_probs(legal, q, eps):
    """Return eps-greedy action probabilities over the legal actions, as a tensor.

    Each legal action gets ``eps / (number of legal actions)``. The remaining ``1 - eps`` is
    split evenly between the legal actions tied for the largest q. With ``eps = 0`` this is
    the greedy policy with ties broken at random.

    Parameters
    ----------
    legal : TensorVariable, shape (..., n_actions)
        1.0 where an action is legal.
    q : TensorVariable, shape (..., n_actions)
        Action values.
    eps : TensorVariable, shape (...)
        Exploration rate for each row.

    Returns
    -------
    TensorVariable, shape (..., n_actions)
        pi(a|s) for each row. Each row sums to 1.
    """
    q_legal = pt.where(legal > 0, q, NEG_INF)
    is_max = legal * pt.eq(q_legal, q_legal.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return (legal * (eps / legal.sum(axis=-1))[..., None]
            + is_max * ((1.0 - eps)[..., None] / is_max.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)))


def make_dyna(env, planner, n_planning, seed, keep_Q_history=False):
    """Compile a batched tabular Dyna learner.

    Each step of the scan is one real time step. In each step, the agent acts, updates Q
    from the real transition, updates its model, and then performs `n_planning` planning
    updates. The transition probabilities P and the reward table are inputs to the compiled
    function, so the environment can change between calls. The `env` argument fixes only
    the table sizes, the terminal states, and the start distribution.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        Supplies n_states, n_actions, terminal, legal_actions, start and name. Its P and
        reward tables are not used here; they are passed to the compiled function.
    planner : {'dyna_q', 'dyna_q_plus', 'prioritized'}
        - 'dyna_q' plans from random previously tried (S, A) pairs.
        - 'dyna_q_plus' plans from any legal action in a seen state and
           adds the bonus kappa * sqrt(tau) to the modeled reward.
        - 'prioritized' does not perform direct RL update;
          real and predecessor pairs go into a priority queue that planning pops from.
    n_planning : int
        Planning updates per real time step. 0 gives plain Q-learning.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator. The generator advances on every call, so
        successive calls continue one random stream.
    keep_Q_history : bool, default False
        Also return Q after every time step.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(P, reward, s, Q, model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, priority, t,
        alpha, eps, gamma, kappa, theta, n_steps)``, with

        - P: (n_states, n_actions, n_states) transition probabilities
        - reward: (n_states, n_actions) reward for each (S, A)
        - s: (n_runs,) int64 current state of each run
        - Q, model_reward, tried, last_tried, priority: (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
        - model_next: (n_runs, n_states, n_actions) int64
        - t: float, real time steps so far
        - alpha, eps: (n_runs,) step size and exploration rate per run
        - gamma, kappa, theta: float discount, Dyna-Q+ bonus scale, queue threshold
        - n_steps: int, real time steps to run

        The function first returns the agent's state after the last step: s, Q,
        model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, priority, and t. It then returns
        three arrays of shape (n_steps, n_runs): R, done, and n_updates. The done array
        is 1.0 at each step where an episode ended. The n_updates array counts the direct
        and planning updates made at each step. If `keep_Q_history` is True, a final
        output holds Q after every step, with shape (n_steps, n_runs, n_states, n_actions).

    Notes
    -----
    When a run reaches a terminal state, it restarts from the start distribution within
    the same step. The output is therefore one continuous stream of time steps per run,
    and the `done` array marks where to split it into episodes. Only 'dyna_q_plus' uses
    kappa, and only 'prioritized' uses theta. The other planners accept these arguments
    and ignore them, so all three compiled functions share the same signature.

    """

    not_terminal = pt.as_tensor_variable((~env.terminal).astype("float64"))
    legal_actions = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    start_distribution = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.start)
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name=f"rng_{planner}{n_planning}_{env.name}")

    P = pt.dtensor3("P")
    reward = pt.dmatrix("reward")
    s_in = pt.lvector("s")
    Q_in = pt.dtensor3("Q")
    model_next_in = pt.ltensor3("model_next")
    model_reward_in = pt.dtensor3("model_reward")
    tried_in = pt.dtensor3("tried")
    last_tried_in = pt.dtensor3("last_tried")
    priority_in = pt.dtensor3("priority")
    t_in = pt.dscalar("t")
    alpha = pt.dvector("alpha")
    eps = pt.dvector("eps")
    gamma = pt.dscalar("gamma")
    kappa = pt.dscalar("kappa")
    theta = pt.dscalar("theta")
    n_steps = pt.iscalar("n_steps")

    def max_q(Q, s):
        "max over the legal a of Q(s, a), with each run's own s -> (n_runs,)"
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        return pt.where(legal_actions[s] > 0, Q[runs, s], NEG_INF).max(axis=-1)

    def q_learning_update(Q, s, a, r, s_next, weight):
        """One-step Q-learning on one transition per run.

            Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + weight * alpha * (r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)),

        where the max is 0 when s' is terminal.

        Parameters
        ----------
        Q : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values before the update.
        s, a, s_next : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_runs,)
            The transition of each run.
        r : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            Its reward.
        weight : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,) or float
            Scales the step. 1.0 for a normal update; 0.0 turns the update off for that run.

        Returns
        -------
        TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values after the update.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        target = r + gamma * not_terminal[s_next] * max_q(Q, s_next)
        return pt.inc_subtensor(Q[runs, s, a], weight * alpha * (target - Q[runs, s, a]))

    def plan_dyna(rng, Q, priority, model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, t):
        """Step (f) of Dyna-Q and Dyna-Q+: one simulated transition, one Q-learning update.

        A state the agent has seen is picked uniformly. Dyna-Q then picks an action already
        tried there; Dyna-Q+ picks any legal action. The model supplies (R, S'). Dyna-Q+ adds
        the exploration bonus ``kappa * sqrt(tau)`` to R, where tau = t - last_tried(s, a) is
        the number of time steps since the pair was last tried for real.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        Q : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values.
        priority : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Unused here. Passed through so both planners share one scan signature.
        model_next, model_reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            The learned model: the last S' and R seen after each (s, a).
        tried : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            1.0 once (s, a) has been taken for real.
        last_tried : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            The time step at which (s, a) was last taken.
        t : TensorVariable, scalar
            The current time step.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, Q, priority
            The advanced generator, the updated Q, and the unchanged priority.
        did_update : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            1.0 for every run: each run made one update.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        seen = tried.max(axis=2) # previously observed states
        rng, s = rng.categorical(p=seen / seen.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))

        if planner == "dyna_q": # an action previously taken in S
            candidates = tried[runs, s]
        else: # Dyna-Q+: any action at all
            candidates = legal_actions[s]

        rng, a = rng.categorical(p=candidates / candidates.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
        r = model_reward[runs, s, a]

        if planner == "dyna_q_plus": # the exploration bonus kappa sqrt(tau)
            r = r + kappa * pt.sqrt(t - last_tried[runs, s, a])

        Q = q_learning_update(Q, s, a, r, model_next[runs, s, a], 1.0)
        return rng, Q, priority, pt.ones_like(alpha)

    def plan_prioritized(rng, Q, priority, model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, t):
        """One planning step of prioritized sweeping.

        Pop the (s, a) with the highest priority and apply a Q-learning update with the
        model's (R, S'). Then, for every tried pair (s_bar, a_bar) that the model says leads
        to s, compute

            change = | R_bar + gamma * max_a Q(s, a) - Q(s_bar, a_bar) |

        and queue the pair with priority ``change`` if ``change > theta``. A pair already in
        the queue keeps the higher of its two priorities. A run whose queue is empty does
        nothing this step.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state. Unused here, passed through.
        Q : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            Action values.
        priority : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            The queue: the priority of each (s, a), or 0.0 if it is not queued.
        model_next, model_reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            The learned model: the last S' and R seen after each (s, a).
        tried : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
            1.0 once (s, a) has been taken for real.
        last_tried, t
            Unused here. Passed in so both planners share one scan signature.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, Q, priority
            The generator, the updated Q, and the updated queue.
        did_update : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            1.0 for runs that popped a pair, 0.0 for runs whose queue was empty.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        flat = priority.reshape((Q.shape[0], -1))

        top = pt.argmax(flat, axis=1)
        s, a = top // env.n_actions, top % env.n_actions

        nonempty = pt.gt(flat.max(axis=1), 0.0).astype("float64") # 0: nothing to do this step
        priority = pt.set_subtensor(priority[runs, s, a], 0.0)

        Q = q_learning_update(Q, s, a, model_reward[runs, s, a], model_next[runs, s, a], nonempty)

        leads_to_s = tried * pt.eq(model_next, s[:, None, None]) # all (S_bar, A_bar) -> S
        change = pt.abs(model_reward + gamma * max_q(Q, s)[:, None, None] - Q)
        insert = nonempty[:, None, None] * leads_to_s * pt.gt(change, theta)
        priority = pt.maximum(priority, insert * change) # keep the higher priority
        return rng, Q, priority, nonempty

    plan = plan_prioritized if planner == "prioritized" else plan_dyna

    def time_step(
            rng,
            s,
            Q,
            model_next,
            model_reward,
            tried,
            last_tried,
            priority,
            t,
            P,
            reward,
            alpha,
            eps,
            gamma,
            kappa,
            theta
    ):
        """One real time step of tabular Dyna, in every run at once.

        Following the book's tabular Dyna-Q box:
        (b)-(c) choose A eps-greedily from Q and take it, observing R and S';
        (d) direct RL, a Q-learning update on the real transition (prioritized sweeping queues the pair instead);
        (e) model learning, storing Model(S, A) <- (R, S'); (f) ``n_planning`` planning steps. A run that reaches a
        terminal state restarts from the start distribution in the same step.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        s : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_runs,)
            The current state of each run.
        Q, model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, priority : TensorVariable
            The agent's tables, each of shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions). See `DynaAgent`.
        t : TensorVariable, scalar
            Real time steps so far.
        P : TensorVariable, shape (n_states, n_actions, n_states)
            The real environment's transition probabilities.
        reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_states, n_actions)
            The real environment's rewards.
        alpha, eps : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            Step size and exploration rate of each run.
        gamma, kappa, theta : TensorVariable, scalar
            Discount factor, Dyna-Q+ bonus scale, and prioritized-sweeping queue threshold.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, s_next, Q, model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, priority, t
            The agent's state after the step, in the same order as the inputs.
        r : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            The real reward received.
        done : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            1.0 where the step ended an episode.
        n_updates : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs,)
            Direct plus planning updates made in this step.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(Q.shape[0])
        # (b), (c): act in the real world
        rng, a = rng.categorical(p=eps_greedy_probs(legal_actions[s], Q[runs, s], eps))
        rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a])
        r = reward[s, a]
        t = t + 1.0

        if planner == "prioritized": # no direct update: the real pair joins the queue instead
            change = pt.abs(r + gamma * not_terminal[s_next] * max_q(Q, s_next) - Q[runs, s, a])
            priority = pt.set_subtensor(
                priority[runs, s, a],
                pt.maximum(priority[runs, s, a], change * pt.gt(change, theta))
            )
            n_updates = pt.zeros_like(alpha)
        else: # (d): direct RL
            Q = q_learning_update(Q, s, a, r, s_next, 1.0)
            n_updates = pt.ones_like(alpha)

        # (e): model learning
        if planner == "dyna_q_plus": # a first visit to s models its untried actions as no-ops
            first_visit = pt.eq(tried[runs, s].max(axis=1), 0.0)
            model_next = pt.set_subtensor(
                model_next[runs, s],
                pt.where(first_visit[:, None], s[:, None], model_next[runs, s])
            )

        model_next = pt.set_subtensor(model_next[runs, s, a], s_next)
        model_reward = pt.set_subtensor(model_reward[runs, s, a], r)
        tried = pt.set_subtensor(tried[runs, s, a], 1.0)
        last_tried = pt.set_subtensor(last_tried[runs, s, a], t)

        # (f): planning
        if n_planning > 0:
            rng, Q_seq, priority_seq, did_update = pytensor.scan(
                fn=plan,
                outputs_info=[rng, Q, priority, None],
                non_sequences=[model_next, model_reward, tried, last_tried, t],
                n_steps=n_planning,
                return_updates=False
            )
            Q, priority = Q_seq[-1], priority_seq[-1]
            n_updates = n_updates + did_update.sum(axis=0)

        done = 1.0 - not_terminal[s_next]
        rng, s_restart = rng.categorical(p=pt.ones((Q.shape[0], 1)) * start_distribution[None, :])
        s_next = pt.where(done > 0, s_restart, s_next) # a finished episode restarts in place
        return (
            rng,
            s_next,
            Q,
            model_next,
            model_reward,
            tried,
            last_tried,
            priority,
            t,
            r,
            done,
            n_updates
        )

    (rng_final, s_seq, Q_seq, model_next_seq, model_reward_seq, tried_seq, last_tried_seq,
     priority_seq, t_seq, R_seq, done_seq, updates_seq) = pytensor.scan(
        fn=time_step,
        outputs_info=[
            rng_shared,
            s_in, Q_in,
            model_next_in,
            model_reward_in,
            tried_in,
            last_tried_in,
            priority_in,
            t_in,
            None,
            None,
            None
        ],
        non_sequences=[P, reward, alpha, eps, gamma, kappa, theta],
        n_steps=n_steps,
        return_updates=False
    )

    inputs = [
        P,
        reward,
        s_in,
        Q_in,
        model_next_in,
        model_reward_in,
        tried_in,
        last_tried_in,
        priority_in,
        t_in,
        alpha,
        eps,
        gamma,
        kappa,
        theta,
        n_steps
    ]

    outputs = [
        s_seq[-1],
        Q_seq[-1],
        model_next_seq[-1],
        model_reward_seq[-1],
        tried_seq[-1],
        last_tried_seq[-1],
        priority_seq[-1],
        t_seq[-1],
        R_seq,
        done_seq,
        updates_seq
    ]

    if keep_Q_history: # scan made Q at every step anyway; keep them all
        outputs.append(Q_seq)

    return pytensor.function(
        inputs,
        outputs,
        updates={rng_shared: rng_final},
        on_unused_input="ignore"
    )


@dataclass
class DynaAgent:
    s: np.ndarray            # (n_runs,) current state
    Q: np.ndarray            # (n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
    model_next: np.ndarray   # the S' last seen after (s, a); s itself until then
    model_reward: np.ndarray # the R last seen after (s, a)
    tried: np.ndarray        # 1 once (s, a) has been taken for real
    last_tried: np.ndarray   # the time step (s, a) was last taken (Dyna-Q+)
    priority: np.ndarray     # the prioritized-sweeping queue; 0 means not queued
    t: float = 0.0           # time steps so far

def fresh_agent(env, n_runs):
    """Return a `DynaAgent` for a batch of runs, that has not acted yet.

    Every run starts at the first start state, with Q = 0, an empty model, and an empty
    queue. Until a pair is tried, the model predicts that it leaves the agent where it is
    with reward 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        Supplies the table sizes and the start state.
    n_runs : int
        Number of independent runs.

    Returns
    -------
    DynaAgent
        Arrays of shape (n_runs,) for ``s`` and (n_runs, n_states, n_actions) for the tables.
    """
    table =(n_runs, env.n_states, env.n_actions)
    stay_put = np.broadcast_to(np.arange(env.n_states)[None, :, None], table).astype("int64")
    return DynaAgent(
        s=np.full(n_runs, int(np.argmax(env.start)), dtype="int64"),
        Q=np.zeros(table),
        model_next=stay_put.copy(),
        model_reward=np.zeros(table),
        tried=np.zeros(table),
        last_tried=np.zeros(table),
        priority=np.zeros(table)
    )

def run_dyna(learner, env, agent, n_steps, alpha, eps, gamma=GAMMA_MAZE, kappa=0.0, theta=0.0):
    """Run a compiled Dyna learner for ``n_steps`` real time steps in `env`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    learner : pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        A learner compiled by `make_dyna`.
    env : Env
        The real environment for these steps. Its ``P`` and ``reward_mean`` are passed to
        the learner, so a later call can use a changed environment.
    agent : DynaAgent
        The agent's state at the start: current states, Q, model, queue and time.
    n_steps : int
        Real time steps to run.
    alpha, eps : float
        Step size and exploration rate, the same for every run.
    gamma : float, default GAMMA_MAZE
        Discount factor.
    kappa : float, default 0.0
        Dyna-Q+ exploration-bonus scale. Used only by 'dyna_q_plus'.
    theta : float, default 0.0
        Prioritized-sweeping queue threshold. Used only by 'prioritized'.

    Returns
    -------
    agent : DynaAgent
        The agent's state after the last step.
    R, done, n_updates : ndarray, shape (n_steps, n_runs)
        The reward at each step, 1.0 where an episode ended, and the updates made.
    Q_history : ndarray, shape (n_steps, n_runs, n_states, n_actions)
        Q after every step. Returned only if the learner was built with ``keep_Q_history``.
    """
    n_runs = len(agent.s)
    out = learner(
        env.P,
        env.reward_mean,
        *[getattr(agent, f.name) for f in fields(agent)],
        np.full(n_runs, alpha),
        np.full(n_runs, eps),
        gamma,
        kappa,
        theta,
        n_steps
    )
    return (DynaAgent(*out[:8]), *out[8:])

def episode_lengths(done, run):
    """Split one run's stream of time steps into its completed episodes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    done : ndarray, shape (n_steps, n_runs)
        1.0 at each step where an episode ended, as returned by `run_dyna`.
    run : int
        Which run.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of int, shape (n_completed_episodes,)
        The number of steps in each completed episode, in order. An unfinished last
        episode is not included.
    """
    ends = np.flatnonzero(done[:, run] > 0)
    return np.diff(np.concatenate([[-1], ends]))

The Dyna Maze
We compare Dyna-Q agents that make \(n = 0\), \(5\) and \(50\) planning updates per real step. Everything else is the same for all three: * \(\alpha = 0.1\) * \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) * \(\gamma = 0.95\) * \(Q\) starting at zero, and * 30 independent runs each.
We record how many steps each of the first 50 episodes took.
Because the learner runs for a fixed number of time steps rather than a fixed number of episodes, each \(n\) gets a time-step budget comfortably larger than 50 episodes should need.

N_RUNS_MAZE, N_EPISODES_MAZE = 30, 50

    learner = make_dyna(dyna_maze, "dyna_q", n, seed=100 + n)
    agent, R, done, n_updates = run_dyna(
        learner,
        dyna_maze,
        fresh_agent(dyna_maze, N_RUNS_MAZE),
        budget,
        ALPHA_MAZE,
        EPS_MAZE
    )

    lengths = [episode_lengths(done, run) for run in range(N_RUNS_MAZE)]
    completed = np.array([len(l) for l in lengths])
    steps_per_episode[n] = np.array([l[:N_EPISODES_MAZE] for l in lengths]).mean(axis=0)

Every agent took between 587 and 872 steps, on average, to finish an episode, because until the goal has been reached, every reward the agent has seen is zero. There is no value anywhere to pass back, so neither learning nor planning can help yet.
After the first episode, the three curves separate completely:

\(n = 50\) has essentially solved the maze after one episode: 40 steps in episode 2, and 17-18 from episode 3 on.
\(n = 5\) needs about five episodes: 150, 68, 37 and 23 steps in episodes 2 to 5.
\(n = 0\), plain one-step Q-learning, still takes 265 steps in episode 5 and 94 in episode 13. It first gets within 2 steps of its final level in episode 29.

All three settle at 16.6-17.5 steps per episode, while the shortest path is 14 steps. The gap is the cost of exploring with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), which makes the agent take a random action about one step in ten. The next figure really highlights why planning makes such a big difference.

def halfway_through_episode_2(n, seed):
    """Run Dyna-Q once on the Dyna maze and return Q halfway through the second episode.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n : int
        Planning steps per real time step. 0 gives plain Q-learning.
    seed : int
        Seed for the learner's random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    Q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values after the step halfway through episode 2.
    first, second : int
        The lengths of episodes 1 and 2, in steps.
    """
    learner = make_dyna(dyna_maze, "dyna_q", n, seed=seed, keep_Q_history=True)
    agent, R, done, n_updates, Q_history = run_dyna(
        learner,
        dyna_maze,
        fresh_agent(dyna_maze, 1),
        6000,
        ALPHA_MAZE,
        EPS_MAZE
    )

    first, second = episode_lengths(done, 0)[:2]
    halfway = first + second // 2
    return Q_history[halfway - 1, 0], first, second

    decided = (Q.max(axis=1) > Q.min(axis=1)).sum()


policy_fig = maze_figure(
    {"without planning" if n == 0 else f"with planning (n = {n})": dyna_maze for n in Q_halfway},
    title="Greedy policies halfway through the second episode"
          "<br><sup>Orange arrow wherever Q prefers one action and blank cells are still all ties</sup>",
    cell_px=40
)
for col, (Q, _, _) in enumerate(Q_halfway.values(), start=1):
    decided = np.flatnonzero(Q.max(axis=1) > Q.min(axis=1)) # only where a greedy action exists
    draw_arrows(policy_fig, dyna_maze, Q.argmax(axis=1), decided, row=1, col=col)

policy_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            



policy_fig = maze_figure(
    {"without planning" if n == 0 else f"with planning (n = {n})": dyna_maze for n in Q_halfway},
    title="Greedy policies halfway through the second episode"
          "<br><sup>Orange arrow wherever Q prefers one action and blank cells are still all ties</sup>",
    cell_px=40,
    theme=GRID_DARK
)
for col, (Q, _, _) in enumerate(Q_halfway.values(), start=1):
    decided = np.flatnonzero(Q.max(axis=1) > Q.min(axis=1)) # only where a greedy action exists
    draw_arrows(policy_fig, dyna_maze, Q.argmax(axis=1), decided, row=1, col=col)

policy_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            


Halfway through the second episode, the agent without planning prefers an action in exactly one state; the cell right next to the goal. It learned that on the very last step of episode 1, when it finally reached \(G\). One-step Q-learning only passes a value back from a state to the state just before it, so the path to the goal gets learned roughly one step per episode. That is why plain Q-learning needed 29 episodes.
Over the same stretch, the agent with planning made 50 planning updates for every real step. The one rewarding transition from episode 1 has been replayed from the model again and again, and each replay can push the value one state further back from the goal. Now 14 states have a preferred action. Together they form a policy that fans out backward from \(G\), down the right-hand side of the maze, toward wherever the agent happens to be wandering.
Without planning, each episode adds only one step to the policy, and with planning, most of the policy is built during the second episode.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
section: A priority queue without a heap
text:
A priority queue without a heap
The usual way to build a priority queue is a heap, a tree-shaped structure of pointers that gets rearranged one element at a time, which obviously doesn’t fit inside a scan. However, our queue can only ever hold state-action pairs, and there is only a fixed number of those. So we can store the queue as an array of priorities with shape (n_runs, n_states, n_actions), where 0 means “not in the queue”. Every queue operation then becomes a whole-array operation:

first(PQueue), the pair with the highest priority, is an argmax over the flattened array, and removing it from the queue sets its entry to 0
all \(\bar S, \bar A\) predicted to lead to \(S\) is the mask tried * (model_next == S): every predecessor at once, with no loop and no list of predecessors to keep up to date
insert, keeping the higher priority is an elementwise maximum.

This is the plan_prioritized branch of make_dyna above. If a run’s queue is empty, its planning step does nothing and reports that it made no update, so the update counts below include only updates that actually happened.
