title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
Prioritized sweeping on mazes
The book compares the two planners on versions of the Dyna maze at increasing resolution, and counts the updates needed until an optimal solution is found. We scale the maze by a factor \(k\): every cell becomes a \(k\times k\) block of cells. The number of states grows as \(k^2\), and the shortest path grows roughly as \(14k\). Both agents make at most \(n = 5\) updates per real step, with \(\alpha = 1\) (the world is deterministic, so a single update gives the exact value), \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\theta = 10^{-4}\).
We run the agents in chunks of 20 real steps. After each chunk we follow the greedy policy from \(S\) and compare the length of its path with \(L^*\), the shortest path length according to the oracle. Requiring the path to be exactly \(L^*\) turns out to measure exploration luck rather than planning. Because the agents explore with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy, some runs settle on a route one or two cells longer than the shortest, because the shortest route goes through pairs they have never tried, and no amount of planning can value a pair that has never been tried. So we count a run as solved once its greedy path is within 20% of \(L^*\), and report how many runs got there within the step budget.

def scaled_dyna_maze(k):
    """Build the Dyna maze at k times the resolution.

    Every cell of the 6 x 9 maze becomes a k x k block, so walls stay walls and the
    shortest path grows about k-fold. The start is the left end of row 2k and the goal
    the top-right corner.

    Parameters
    ----------
    k : int
        The resolution factor. k = 1 gives the original maze.

    Returns
    -------
    Env
        A 6k x 9k maze.
    """
    walls = {(row * k + i, col * k + j) for row, col in DYNA_WALLS for i in range(k) for j in range(k)}
    n_rows, n_cols = 6 * k, 9 * k
    return maze_env(
        f"dyna_maze_x{k}",
        walls,
        start=(2 * k, 0),
        goal=(0, n_cols - 1),
        n_rows=n_rows,
        n_cols=n_cols
    )

def greedy_path_length(env, Q, limit):
    """Count the steps the greedy policy of Q takes from the start to the goal.

    The maze is deterministic, so following the policy once is exact.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        A deterministic maze.
    Q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values. Ties go to the lowest-numbered action.
    limit : int
        Give up after this many steps.

    Returns
    -------
    int
        The path length, or ``limit + 1`` if the policy has not reached the goal by then.
    """
    next_state = env.P.argmax(axis=2) # deterministic world
    s, steps = int(np.argmax(env.start)), 0
    while not env.terminal[s] and steps <= limit:
        s = next_state[s, int(Q[s].argmax())]
        steps += 1
    return steps

N_RUNS_SWEEP, CHUNK_SWEEP, MAX_CHUNKS_SWEEP, TOLERANCE_SWEEP = 10, 20, 3000, 1.2
ALPHA_SWEEP, THETA_SWEEP, N_PLANNING_SWEEP = 1.0, 1e-4, 5

def updates_until_solved(env, planner, shortest, seed):
    """Count the updates each run needs before its greedy path is nearly shortest.

    The agent runs in chunks of ``CHUNK_SWEEP`` real steps, for at most
    ``MAX_CHUNKS_SWEEP`` chunks. After each chunk, a run counts as solved once its greedy
    path is at most ``TOLERANCE_SWEEP * shortest`` steps long. Updates are direct plus
    planning updates.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The maze.
    planner : {'dyna_q', 'prioritized'}
        Which planner to run, with ``N_PLANNING_SWEEP`` planning steps per real step.
    shortest : int
        Length of the shortest path from start to goal.
    seed : int
        Seed for the learner's random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (N_RUNS_SWEEP,)
        For each run, the total updates at the end of the chunk in which it was solved.
        NaN for a run that was never solved.
    """
    learner = make_dyna(env, planner, N_PLANNING_SWEEP, seed=seed)
    agent = fresh_agent(env, N_RUNS_SWEEP)
    total_updates = np.zeros(N_RUNS_SWEEP)
    solved_at = np.full(N_RUNS_SWEEP, np.nan)

    for chunk in range(MAX_CHUNKS_SWEEP):
        agent, _, _, n_updates = run_dyna(
            learner,
            env,
            agent,
            CHUNK_SWEEP,
            ALPHA_SWEEP,
            EPS_MAZE,
            theta=THETA_SWEEP
        )

        total_updates += n_updates.sum(axis=0)

        for run in np.flatnonzero(np.isnan(solved_at)):
            if greedy_path_length(env, agent.Q[run], 2 * shortest) <= TOLERANCE_SWEEP * shortest:
                solved_at[run] = total_updates[run]

        if not np.isnan(solved_at).any():
            break

    return solved_at


planners_sweep = {"prioritized sweeping": "prioritized", "Dyna-Q": "dyna_q"}
sizes_sweep, solved_sweep = [], {label: [] for label in planners_sweep}
for k in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    maze = scaled_dyna_maze(k)
    v_star, _ = exact(maze, GAMMA_MAZE)
    shortest = int(round(1 + np.log(v_star[np.argmax(maze.start)]) / np.log(GAMMA_MAZE)))
    sizes_sweep.append(int((maze.reachable & ~maze.terminal).sum()))

    for label, planner in planners_sweep.items():
        solved = updates_until_solved(maze, planner, shortest, seed=k)
        solved_sweep[label].append(solved)


sweep_fig = go.Figure()

for i, label in enumerate(planners_sweep):
    runs = np.array(solved_sweep[label]) # (n_sizes, n_runs)
    jitter = np.linspace(0.96, 1.04, N_RUNS_SWEEP)

    sweep_fig.add_scatter(
        x=(np.array(sizes_sweep)[:, None] * jitter[None, :]).ravel(),
        y=runs.ravel(),
        mode="markers",
        name=f"{label}, single runs (jittered)",
        legendgroup=label,
        marker=dict(
            size=8,
            color=colors[i],
            opacity=0.45,
            symbol="circle" if i == 0 else "diamond",
            line=dict(color="white", width=1)
        ),
        hoverinfo="skip"
    )

    sweep_fig.add_scatter(
        x=sizes_sweep,
        y=np.nanmedian(runs, axis=1),
        mode="lines+markers",
        name=f"{label}, median",
        legendgroup=label,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5),
        marker=dict(size=10, symbol="circle" if i == 0 else "diamond", line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
        hovertemplate="<b>%{y:,.0f}</b>"
    )

sweep_fig.update_layout(
    title="Updates until the greedy path is within 20% of the shortest path"
          f"<br><sup>the Dyna maze at resolution k = 1 -> 4, {N_RUNS_SWEEP} runs each, "
          f"n = {N_PLANNING_SWEEP} updates per real step</sup>",
    xaxis=dict(title="States in the maze"),
    yaxis=dict(title="Updates (log scale)", type="log"),
    template="plotly_white",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.18, x=0),
    hovermode="x unified",
    margin=dict(t=100, b=100)
)

sweep_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            



sweep_fig = go.Figure()

for i, label in enumerate(planners_sweep):
    runs = np.array(solved_sweep[label]) # (n_sizes, n_runs)
    jitter = np.linspace(0.96, 1.04, N_RUNS_SWEEP)

    sweep_fig.add_scatter(
        x=(np.array(sizes_sweep)[:, None] * jitter[None, :]).ravel(),
        y=runs.ravel(),
        mode="markers",
        name=f"{label}, single runs (jittered)",
        legendgroup=label,
        marker=dict(
            size=8,
            color=colors[i],
            opacity=0.45,
            symbol="circle" if i == 0 else "diamond",
            line=dict(color="white", width=1)
        ),
        hoverinfo="skip"
    )

    sweep_fig.add_scatter(
        x=sizes_sweep,
        y=np.nanmedian(runs, axis=1),
        mode="lines+markers",
        name=f"{label}, median",
        legendgroup=label,
        line=dict(color=colors[i], width=2.5),
        marker=dict(size=10, symbol="circle" if i == 0 else "diamond", line=dict(color="white", width=1)),
        hovertemplate="<b>%{y:,.0f}</b>"
    )

sweep_fig.update_layout(
    title="Updates until the greedy path is within 20% of the shortest path"
          f"<br><sup>the Dyna maze at resolution k = 1 -> 4, {N_RUNS_SWEEP} runs each, "
          f"n = {N_PLANNING_SWEEP} updates per real step</sup>",
    xaxis=dict(title="States in the maze"),
    yaxis=dict(title="Updates (log scale)", type="log"),
    template="plotly_dark",
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="top", y=-0.18, x=0),
    hovermode="x unified",
    margin=dict(t=100, b=100)
)

sweep_fig.show(config=dict(displayModeBar=False))

                            
                                            


Prioritized sweeping needed between 47 and 67 times fewer updates than Dyna-Q at every maze size: 147 against 6,840 on the original maze, and 2,645 against 143,400 on the largest one, with 751 states.
The book reports a factor of 5 to 10, so ours is much larger. The difference comes from our setting, not from an error. With \(\alpha = 1\) in a deterministic maze, a prioritized update is final: it sets the popped pair to its exact backed-up value, and that pair never needs updating again unless the value of the state it leads to changes. So every update prioritized sweeping makes moves information one step further back along a path. Dyna-Q’s uniform choice, by contrast, spends most of its updates on pairs whose targets haven’t changed since they were last updated (updates that change nothing).
Both medians grow roughly in proportion to the number of states. So on these mazes, prioritized sweeping’s advantage is a large constant factor, not a better growth rate.
Three of the 80 runs never met the criterion within 60,000 real steps (one prioritized-sweeping run and two Dyna-Q runs). This is the exploration problem described above. Their greedy route settled on a path more than 20% longer than the shortest, because the shorter one goes through pairs the agent had never tried.






Note



The medians in the figure above are taken over the runs that finished.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
The racetrack environment
The book tests this claim on the racetrack environment. Here is how it works:

The car sits on a grid and has a velocity \((v_{\uparrow}, v_{\rightarrow})\): how many cells it moves up and to the right on each step. Each component is an integer from 0 to 4, and the two cannot both be zero except on the start line.
Each action changes each velocity component by \(-1\), \(0\) or \(+1\), which gives 9 actions. With probability 0.1 the change is ignored and the velocity stays as it was.
The car then moves by its velocity. If its path crosses the finish line, the episode ends. If it leaves the track, it is sent back to a random cell on the start line, at rest.
Every step costs \(-1\), so \(-V(s)\) is the expected number of steps to the finish.







Important



The track below is slightly different than the book’s example, so the state counts differ.


Storing the dynamics as a dense \(P\) would take a \(7543\times9\times7543\) array. Instead we store a successor table, in which, for each \((s, a)\), we store the few states it can lead to and their probabilities. To build the table we trace the car’s straight-line path through the grid for every state, action and noise outcome.






Note



A crash spreads over all six start cells.



TRACK = [
    "###.............F",
    "##..............F",
    "##..............F",
    "#...............F",
    "................F",
    "................F",
    *["..........#######"] * 8,
    *["#.........#######"] * 8,
    *["##........#######"] * 7,
    *["###......########"] * 2,
    "###SSSSSS########",
]
MAX_SPEED, NOISE = 4, 0.1
STEP_REWARD_TRACK = -1.0 # reward on every step until the car crosses the finish line
GAMMA_TRACK = 1.0 # undiscounted, so -V(s) is the expected number of steps to finish
INCREMENTS = [(increment_up, increment_right)
              for increment_up in (-1, 0, 1) for increment_right in (-1, 0, 1)]

@dataclass
class Racetrack:
    grid: np.ndarray        # the track, '.' road, 'S' start line, 'F' finish line, '#' off track
    n_states: int
    n_actions: int
    terminal: int           # the single "crossed the finish line" state
    starts: np.ndarray      # the start-line states, at rest
    successors: np.ndarray  # (n_states, n_actions, width) the states each action can lead to
    probs: np.ndarray       # (n_states, n_actions, width) and their probabilities
    legal: np.ndarray       # (n_states, n_actions)
    cell_of: np.ndarray     # (n_states, 2) the (row, col) of each state; (-1, -1) for terminal

def number_states(grid):
    """Number every non-terminal state of the racetrack.

    A state is ``(row, col, velocity_up, velocity_right)`` on a road or start cell, with
    each velocity component between 0 and MAX_SPEED. The car is at rest, velocity (0, 0),
    only on the start line.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : ndarray of str, shape (n_rows, n_cols)
        The track, one character per cell.

    Returns
    -------
    dict of {(int, int, int, int): int}
        The state id of each ``(row, col, velocity_up, velocity_right)``, numbered from 0.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = grid.shape
    velocities = [
        (velocity_up, velocity_right)
        for velocity_up in range(MAX_SPEED + 1) for velocity_right in range(MAX_SPEED + 1)
    ]

    index = {}
    for row in range(n_rows):
        for col in range(n_cols):
            if grid[row, col] not in ".S":
                continue
            for velocity_up, velocity_right in velocities:
                at_rest = (velocity_up, velocity_right) == (0, 0)
                if not at_rest or grid[row, col] == "S": # at rest only on the start states
                    index[(row, col, velocity_up, velocity_right)] = len(index)
    return index

def accelerate(velocity, increment):
    """Add an action's increment to the velocity, keeping each component between 0 and MAX_SPEED.

    Parameters
    ----------
    velocity : (int, int)
        ``(velocity_up, velocity_right)`` before the action.
    increment : (int, int)
        ``(increment_up, increment_right)``, each -1, 0 or +1.

    Returns
    -------
    (int, int)
        The new ``(velocity_up, velocity_right)``.
    """
    velocity_up, velocity_right = velocity
    increment_up, increment_right = increment
    new_velocity_up = min(max(velocity_up + increment_up, 0), MAX_SPEED)
    new_velocity_right = min(max(velocity_right + increment_right, 0), MAX_SPEED)
    return new_velocity_up, new_velocity_right

def drive(grid, row, col, velocity):
    """Move the car one time step at a constant velocity, checking its path for crashes.

    The straight-line path is checked every quarter of a cell along the way, not only at
    the landing cell, so a fast car does not skip over off-track cells or the finish line.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : ndarray of str, shape (n_rows, n_cols)
        The track.
    row, col : int
        Where the car starts the step.
    velocity : (int, int)
        ``(velocity_up, velocity_right)``. Up means toward row 0.

    Returns
    -------
    "crash", "finish", or (int, int)
        "crash" if the path leaves the track or touches a "#", "finish" if it reaches an
        "F" first, otherwise the new ``(row, col)``.
    """
    n_rows, n_cols = grid.shape
    velocity_up, velocity_right = velocity
    for fraction in np.linspace(0, 1, 4 * max(velocity_up, velocity_right) + 1)[1:]:
        path_row = int(round(row - fraction * velocity_up))
        path_col = int(round(col + fraction * velocity_right))
        inside = 0 <= path_row < n_rows and 0 <= path_col < n_cols
        if not inside or grid[path_row, path_col] == "#":
            return "crash"
        if grid[path_row, path_col] == "F":
            return "finish"
    return row - velocity_up, col + velocity_right

def landing_distribution(grid, index, starts, row, col, velocity):
    """Return where one move at this velocity leaves the car, as {state: probability}.

    Crossing the finish leads to the terminal state. A crash sends the car back to a
    start state chosen uniformly, at rest. Otherwise the car lands on its new cell with
    the same velocity.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : ndarray of str, shape (n_rows, n_cols)
        The track.
    index : dict
        State ids, from `number_states`. The terminal state is numbered ``len(index)``.
    starts : list of int
        The start states.
    row, col : int
        Where the car starts the step.
    velocity : (int, int)
        The velocity used for this move.

    Returns
    -------
    dict of {int: float}
        The probability of each next state.
    """
    result = drive(grid, row, col, velocity)
    if result == "finish":
        return {len(index): 1.0} # the terminal state, numbered last
    if result == "crash":
        return {start_state: 1.0 / len(starts) for start_state in starts}
    return {index[(*result, *velocity)]: 1.0}

def action_distribution(grid, index, starts, row, col, velocity, increment):
    """Return the distribution of next states for one action, or None if it is illegal.

    With probability 1 - NOISE the increments apply; with probability NOISE they fail and
    the car moves at its old velocity. An action that brings the car to rest off the start
    line is illegal.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : ndarray of str, shape (n_rows, n_cols)
        The track.
    index : dict
        State ids, from `number_states`.
    starts : list of int
        The start states.
    row, col : int
        The car's cell.
    velocity : (int, int)
        The car's velocity before the action.
    increment : (int, int)
        The action: ``(increment_up, increment_right)``.

    Returns
    -------
    dict of {int: float} or None
        The probability of each next state, or None for an illegal action.
    """
    new_velocity = accelerate(velocity, increment)
    if new_velocity == (0, 0) and grid[row, col] != "S":
        return None # illegal

    distribution = {}
    # with probability NOISE the increments fail and the velocity stays the same
    for probability, actual_velocity in ((1 - NOISE, new_velocity), (NOISE, velocity)):
        landing = landing_distribution(grid, index, starts, row, col, actual_velocity)
        for s_next, landing_probability in landing.items():
            distribution.setdefault(s_next, 0.0)
            distribution[s_next] += probability * landing_probability
    return distribution

def successor_table(outcomes, n_states, n_actions):
    """Pack the {next state: probability} of every (s, a) into fixed-width arrays.

    The racetrack has too many states for a dense (n_states, n_actions, n_states) table,
    but each (s, a) has only a few possible next states. So each (s, a) gets ``width``
    slots: slot i holds one next state and its probability. Unused slots point at the
    terminal state with probability 0. The terminal state is last and absorbs.

    Parameters
    ----------
    outcomes : dict of {(int, int): dict of {int: float}}
        The distribution of next states for each legal (s, a).
    n_states, n_actions : int
        Sizes of the tables.

    Returns
    -------
    successors : ndarray of int, shape (n_states, n_actions, width)
        The next state in each slot.
    probs : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions, width)
        Its probability.
    """
    terminal = n_states - 1
    width = max(len(distribution) for distribution in outcomes.values())
    # unused slots point at the terminal state with probability 0
    successors = np.full((n_states, n_actions, width), terminal, dtype="int64")
    probs = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, width))
    for (s, a), distribution in outcomes.items():
        for slot, (s_next, probability) in enumerate(distribution.items()):
            successors[s, a, slot], probs[s, a, slot] = s_next, probability
    probs[terminal, :, 0] = 1.0 # the terminal state absorbs
    return successors, probs

def build_racetrack(track):
    """Build the racetrack MDP of the book's Exercise 5.12, used in Example 8.6.

    Every step earns STEP_REWARD_TRACK until the car crosses the finish line.

    Parameters
    ----------
    track : list of str
        The track, one string per row: "." road, "S" start line, "F" finish line,
        "#" off the track.

    Returns
    -------
    Racetrack
        The states, the legal actions, and the next-state table from `successor_table`.
        The terminal state is numbered last.
    """
    grid =np.array([list(row) for row in track])
    index = number_states(grid)
    terminal = len(index)
    n_states, n_actions = terminal + 1, len(INCREMENTS)
    starts = [s for (row, col, velocity_up, velocity_right), s in index.items()
              if (velocity_up, velocity_right) == (0, 0)]

    legal = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    legal[terminal] = 1.0
    outcomes = {}
    cell_of = np.full((n_states, 2), -1)
    for (row, col, velocity_up, velocity_right), s in index.items():
        cell_of[s] = row, col
        for a, increment in enumerate(INCREMENTS):
            distribution = action_distribution(
                grid,
                index,
                starts,
                row,
                col,
                (velocity_up, velocity_right),
                increment
            )

            if distribution is not None:
                legal[s, a] = 1.0
                outcomes[(s, a)] = distribution

    successors, probs = successor_table(outcomes, n_states, n_actions)
    return Racetrack(
        grid,
        n_states,
        n_actions,
        terminal,
        np.array(starts),
        successors,
        probs,
        legal,
        cell_of
    )

racetrack = build_racetrack(TRACK)
print("\n".join(TRACK))
print(f"\n{racetrack.n_states} states, {racetrack.n_actions} actions, at most "
      f"{racetrack.successors.shape[2]} successors per (s, a), {len(racetrack.starts)} start states")

#...............F
................F
................F
..........#######

..........#######

We need three compiled tools on the racetrack:

In-place value iteration (sweep)
Real-Time Dynamic Programming (rtdp)
An exact grader (greedy_policy_value).

Each one gets its own cell below, just before it is first used. All three rest on the same expected update, so that comes first.
racetrack_tensors wraps the successor table as constant tensors. backed_up(tensors, V, s) then computes the expected update for every action at a batch of states, by reading the successor table:
\[
q(s, a) \;=\; \sum_{s'} p(s' \mid s, a)\left[-1 + V(s')\right].
\]
The \(-1\) is the reward on every step (STEP_REWARD_TRACK). There is no discounting (GAMMA_TRACK \(= 1\)), so it multiplies \(V(s')\) by 1. The batch of states can be one state per run (RTDP), a single state (the in-place sweep), or every state at once (the grader).

@dataclass
class TrackTensors:
    successors: pt.TensorVariable    # (n_states, n_actions, width) the states each action can lead to
    probs: pt.TensorVariable         # (n_states, n_actions, width) and their probabilities
    legal: pt.TensorVariable         # (n_states, n_actions) 1.0 where the action is allowed
    not_terminal: pt.TensorVariable  # (n_states,) 0.0 at the terminal state, 1.0 elsewhere
    starts: pt.TensorVariable        # (n_starts,) the start-line states, at rest
    terminal: int                    # the single "crossed the finish line" state
    n_states: int

def racetrack_tensors(track):
    """Wrap the racetrack's tables as constant tensors, for the compiled tools below.

    Parameters
    ----------
    track : Racetrack
        The racetrack MDP, from `build_racetrack`.

    Returns
    -------
    TrackTensors
        The successor table, the legal actions, the terminal mask and the start states.
    """
    return TrackTensors(
        successors=pt.as_tensor_variable(track.successors),
        probs=pt.as_tensor_variable(track.probs),
        legal=pt.as_tensor_variable(track.legal),
        not_terminal=pt.as_tensor_variable((np.arange(track.n_states) != track.terminal).astype("float64")),
        starts=pt.as_tensor_variable(track.starts),
        terminal=track.terminal,
        n_states=track.n_states
    )

def backed_up(tensors, V, s):
    """Back up every action at a batch of states, with the one-step lookahead.

        q(s, a) = sum_s' p(s'|s, a) [ STEP_REWARD_TRACK + GAMMA_TRACK * V(s') ]

    Every step costs 1 and there is no discounting. So if V is the value of some policy,
    -q(s, a) is the expected number of steps to the finish when taking a and then
    following that policy.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tensors : TrackTensors
        The racetrack's tables.
    V : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states)
        State values, one row per run.
    s : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_runs,) or (n_runs, n_batch)
        The states to back up in each run: one per run (RTDP, in-place sweeps), or a
        batch per run, e.g. every state (grading a greedy policy).

    Returns
    -------
    TensorVariable, shape s.shape + (n_actions,)
        q(s, a) for every action, or NEG_INF where the action is illegal, so that a max
        over actions never picks one.
    """
    runs = pt.shape_padright(pt.arange(V.shape[0]), s.ndim + 1) # broadcasts against successors[s]
    next_values = V[runs, tensors.successors[s]] # s.shape + (n_actions, width)
    q = (tensors.probs[s] * (STEP_REWARD_TRACK + GAMMA_TRACK * next_values)).sum(axis=-1)
    return pt.where(tensors.legal[s] > 0, q, NEG_INF)

sweep is the Dynamic Programming chapter’s in-place (Gauss-Seidel) value iteration. “In place” means each state’s new value is written into \(V\) straight away, so states later in the same sweep already use it. It is a scan over a list of states, where set_subtensor writes each new value back into \(V\) before the next state is updated.

def make_gauss_seidel_sweep(tensors):
    """Compile one in-place (Gauss-Seidel) sweep of value iteration over a list of states.

    The states are updated one after another, each with V(s) <- max_a q(s, a), and each new
    value is written into V before the next state is updated. The terminal state stays at 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tensors : TrackTensors
        The racetrack's tables.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``sweep(V, order) -> (V_new, largest_change)``, with ``V`` of shape (n_states,) and
        ``order`` the states to update, in order. ``largest_change`` is the largest
        ``|V_new(s) - V(s)|`` over all states.
    """
    V_in = pt.dvector("V")
    order = pt.lvector("order")

    def gauss_seidel_update(s, V):
        "V(s) <- max_a q(s, a), using the newest V; the terminal state stays at 0"
        q = backed_up(tensors, V[None, :], s[None])[0]
        return pt.set_subtensor(V[s], tensors.not_terminal[s] * q.max())

    V_seq = pytensor.scan(
        fn=gauss_seidel_update,
        sequences=order,
        outputs_info=V_in,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return pytensor.function(
        [V_in, order],
        [V_seq[-1], pt.abs(V_seq[-1] - V_in).max()]
    )

First, the answer key, and the two sets of states that RTDP is all about:

\(v_*\) comes from running in-place sweeps until nothing changes at all, so it is exact.
The reachable states are those that any policy can reach from the start line.
The relevant states are those that some optimal policy can reach. We find them with a breadth-first search from the start line that follows only optimal actions (those within \(10^{-9}\) of the best).


def closure(track, from_states, allowed):
    """Find every state reachable from `from_states` using only the allowed (s, a) pairs.

    A breadth-first search over the racetrack's next-state table.

    Parameters
    ----------
    track : Racetrack
        The racetrack MDP.
    from_states : array_like of int
        Where the search starts.
    allowed : ndarray of bool, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The actions the search may follow in each state, e.g. the legal actions or only
        the optimal ones.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray of bool, shape (n_states,)
        True for every state found, including `from_states`.
    """
    found = np.zeros(track.n_states, dtype=bool)
    found[from_states] = True

    while True:
        edges = (track.probs > 0) & allowed[:, :, None] & found[:, None, None]
        grown = found.copy()
        grown[track.successors[edges]] = True
        if grown.sum() == found.sum():
            return found
        found = grown

greedy_policy_value is how we grade both sweeping DP and RTDP. The grade is the value of a policy (the greedy policy of the current \(V\)), so it needs one more scan. First it finds that policy with backed_up at every state. Then it runs iterative policy evaluation over the successor table, for 600 sweeps. Under a good policy an episode lasts about a dozen steps, so after 600 sweeps the remaining error is far below \(10^{-6}\).






Note



A policy that never finishes ends up with a value of about \(-600\).



def make_greedy_policy_value(tensors, eval_sweeps=600):
    """Compile the exact grader: the value of the greedy policy of V, batched over runs.

    The greedy policy picks, in every state, the legal action with the largest
    `backed_up` value (ties go to the lowest-numbered action). Its value comes from
    ``eval_sweeps`` synchronous sweeps of iterative policy evaluation from v = 0,

        v(s) <- sum_s' p(s'|s, pi(s)) [ STEP_REWARD_TRACK + GAMMA_TRACK * v(s') ],

    with the terminal state held at 0.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tensors : TrackTensors
        The racetrack's tables.
    eval_sweeps : int, default 600
        Sweeps of policy evaluation. A policy that never finishes gets value about
        ``-eval_sweeps``.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``greedy_policy_value(V_batch) -> v``. Both have shape (n_runs, n_states).
    """
    V_batch = pt.dmatrix("V_batch")
    runs = pt.arange(V_batch.shape[0])
    every_state = pt.zeros((V_batch.shape[0], 1), dtype="int64") + pt.arange(tensors.n_states)[None, :]
    pi = backed_up(tensors, V_batch, every_state).argmax(axis=-1) # (n_runs, n_states)
    policy_successors = tensors.successors[every_state, pi] # (n_runs, n_states, width)
    policy_probs = tensors.probs[every_state, pi]

    def evaluation_sweep(v):
        "v(s) <- sum_s' p(s'|s, pi(s)) [STEP_REWARD_TRACK + GAMMA_TRACK * v(s')]; terminal stays 0"
        next_values = v[runs[:, None, None], policy_successors]
        return tensors.not_terminal * (policy_probs * (STEP_REWARD_TRACK + GAMMA_TRACK * next_values)).sum(axis=-1)

    v_seq = pytensor.scan(
        fn=evaluation_sweep,
        outputs_info=pt.zeros_like(V_batch),
        n_steps=eval_sweeps,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return pytensor.function([V_batch], v_seq[-1])

How many sweeps value iteration needs depends on the order in which it visits the states. With in-place updates, a new value is used right away by every state updated after it in the same sweep, so information travels quickly in the direction of the sweep and slowly against it. On the racetrack, value flows backward from the finish line, because a state’s value depends on the states the car reaches next. Our state numbering happens to run from the top row of the track, next to the finish line, down to the start line (the most favorable order there is). So we try three orders: that one, its reverse, and a random shuffle.
Each run stops when a whole sweep changes no value by more than \(10^{-4}\). We also record the quantity that actually matters, which we call the shortfall. The shortfall measures how much worse the greedy policy is compared to the optimal policy, starting from the start line. It is the mean over the six start states of \(v_*(s) - v_{\pi_V}(s)\), where \(\pi_V\) is the greedy policy of the current \(V\). It is measured in expected extra steps to the finish, and we compute it exactly every quarter sweep.

def start_shortfall(V):
    """Measure how far the greedy policy of V falls short of optimal, from the start line.

    The shortfall of a start state s is v_*(s) - v_greedy(s), the expected number of extra
    steps the greedy policy of V takes to finish. It is averaged over the start line.

    Parameters
    ----------
    V : ndarray, shape (n_states,) or (n_runs, n_states)
        State values, one row per run.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_runs,)
        The mean shortfall for each row of V. 0 means the greedy policy is optimal.
    """
    v = greedy_policy_value(np.atleast_2d(V))
    return (v_star_track[racetrack.starts] - v[:, racetrack.starts]).mean(axis=1)

rtdp is a flat scan over time steps, with several runs computed side by side. At each step it updates \(V(S_t)\) with the same backup, picks the greedy action, samples what happens, and restarts on the start line when the car crosses the finish line. Ties between equally good actions are broken at random, using eps_greedy_probs with \(\varepsilon = 0\). It also counts how many times each state has been updated.

def make_rtdp(tensors, seed):
    """Compile batched RTDP: value-iteration updates along greedy trajectories.

    Each time step updates the current state only, V(s) <- max_a q(s, a), then takes a
    greedy action (ties broken at random), samples the next state from the model, and
    restarts at a random start state when the car finishes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tensors : TrackTensors
        The racetrack's tables.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``rtdp(V_init, counts_init, s_init, n_checkpoints, steps_per_checkpoint)
        -> (V, counts, episodes)``. The inputs have shapes (n_runs, n_states),
        (n_runs, n_states) and (n_runs,). The outputs have shapes
        (n_checkpoints, n_runs, n_states) for V and the per-state update counts, and
        (n_checkpoints, n_runs) for the episodes finished in each checkpoint.
    """
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name="rng_rtdp")
    V_init = pt.dmatrix("V0")
    counts_init = pt.dmatrix("counts0")
    s_init = pt.lvector("s0")
    n_checkpoints = pt.iscalar("n_checkpoints")
    steps_per_checkpoint = pt.iscalar("k")

    def rtdp_step(rng, s, V, counts):
        """One time step of RTDP in every run.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        s : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_runs,)
            The current state of each run.
        V : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states)
            State values.
        counts : TensorVariable, shape (n_runs, n_states)
            How many times each state has been updated.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, s_next, V, counts
            The advanced generator, the next state, and the updated V and counts.
        done : TensorVariable of bool, shape (n_runs,)
            True where the car crossed the finish line on this step.
        """
        runs = pt.arange(V.shape[0])
        q = backed_up(tensors, V, s)
        V = pt.set_subtensor(V[runs, s], q.max(axis=1)) # the value-iteration update
        counts = pt.inc_subtensor(counts[runs, s], 1.0)
        greedy = eps_greedy_probs(tensors.legal[s], q, eps=pt.zeros_like(q[:, 0])) # eps = 0: always greedy
        rng, a = rng.categorical(p=greedy)
        rng, outcome = rng.categorical(p=tensors.probs[s, a])
        s_next = tensors.successors[s, a, outcome]
        done = pt.eq(s_next, tensors.terminal)
        rng, restart = rng.integers(0, tensors.starts.shape[0], size=s.shape)
        return rng, pt.where(done, tensors.starts[restart], s_next), V, counts, done

    def checkpoint(rng, s, V, counts, k):
        "k RTDP steps; return the final state and the episodes finished along the way"
        rng, s_seq, V_seq, counts_seq, done_seq = pytensor.scan(
            fn=rtdp_step,
            outputs_info=[rng, s, V, counts, None],
            n_steps=k,
            return_updates=False
        )
        return rng, s_seq[-1], V_seq[-1], counts_seq[-1], done_seq.sum(axis=0)

    rng_final, _, V_out, counts_out, episodes_out = pytensor.scan(
        fn=checkpoint,
        outputs_info=[rng_shared, s_init, V_init, counts_init, None],
        non_sequences=[steps_per_checkpoint],
        n_steps=n_checkpoints,
        return_updates=False
    )
    return pytensor.function(
        [V_init, counts_init, s_init, n_checkpoints, steps_per_checkpoint],
        [V_out, counts_out, episodes_out],
        updates={rng_shared: rng_final}
    )

def first_below(tol):
    """Find, for each RTDP run, the first checkpoint at which its shortfall is below `tol`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    tol : float
        The shortfall threshold, in expected extra steps.

    Returns
    -------
    updates, episodes : list of float, length N_RUNS_RTDP
        The updates made and the episodes finished by that checkpoint, for each run.
        NaN for a run that never got below `tol`.
    """
    hits = [np.argmax(shortfall_rtdp[:, run] < tol) if (shortfall_rtdp[:, run] < tol).any() else None
            for run in range(N_RUNS_RTDP)]
    below_updates = [updates_rtdp[h] if h is not None else np.nan for h in hits]
    below_episodes = [episodes_so_far[h, run] if h is not None else np.nan for run, h in enumerate(hits)]
    return below_updates, below_episodes

Random-order DP needs 28 sweeps to meet its stopping rule. RTDP leaves most states almost untouched: 92% were updated at most 100 times, and 73% at most 10 times (the book: 98% and 81%), and 0.7% were never updated at all (the book: 3.2%).
The heat map on the right shows where RTDP’s updates went, and it has a striking stripe pattern. On the long straight the car travels three or four cells per step, so it only ever lands on every third or fourth row. Those rows get five to eight times as many updates as the rows it flies over. In the turn, the cells the car swings through get thousands of updates, while the far-left corner of the top section gets none at all.
How much computation each method needed for this experiment does not agree with the book.

By the book’s criteria, RTDP wins. DP’s stopping rule (no value changes by more than \(10^{-4}\) in a sweep) is met after 76,244 updates. RTDP’s greedy policy gets within 0.1 expected steps of optimal after a median of 45,000 updates (2,670 episodes). This is the book’s kind of comparison - DP run until its convergence test passes, RTDP run until its performance stops improving - and by it RTDP needs about 60% of the updates.
According to the oracle, DP was actually done much earlier. DP’s greedy policy was within 0.1 steps of optimal after 32,000 updates, less than halfway to its own stopping rule, and DP is ahead of RTDP at every tolerance. The two stopping rules measure different things. DP’s measures its values, which keep changing long after the policy has stopped changing; RTDP’s measures its policy. Without an oracle, neither method could see the other’s number.
RTDP doesn’t save more because so many states are relevant. On our track, 48% of the reachable states are relevant. In the book’s example it is 599 of 9,115, under 7%. RTDP’s advantage comes from skipping the states that no optimal policy needs, and our track has comparatively few of them to skip. A track with a large region that good driving never enters would favor RTDP more.

The convergence theorem does hold. After 150,000 updates, RTDP’s median shortfall is \(0.007\) steps, and only 0.08% of the relevant states were never updated, against 1.2% of the irrelevant ones. Even so, 2 of the 10 runs still hadn’t reached a shortfall of 0.01. RTDP’s final stretch is slow, because it has to pin down the values of rarely visited states well enough to tell nearly tied actions apart.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
section: How to grade a decision-time planner
text:
How to grade a decision-time planner
A decision-time planner doesn’t store a table, so there is nothing to compare with \(q_*\) directly. But it does define a policy: in state \(s\), the probability that the planner, run from scratch, with fresh random numbers, returns action \(a\). And because the planner starts from scratch at every step, that probability depends only on the current state. In other words the policy is Markov, so the DP oracle can evaluate it exactly.
So we run each planner \(K\) times from every state, count how often it picks each action to get an empirical \(\pi(a\mid s)\), and pass that policy to exact to get \(v_\pi\). That gives us three evaluation metrics:

\(v_\pi(S)\), the value at the start state
the mean shortfall \(\frac1{37}\sum_s\left[v_*(s) - v_\pi(s)\right]\): how far below optimal the policy is, averaged over the 37 states the agent can be in
optimal choices: the probability the planner puts on optimal actions, averaged over those same states.


GAMMA_CLIFF = 0.95
start_cliff = int(np.argmax(cliff.start))
live_cliff = cliff.reachable & ~cliff.terminal
roots_cliff = np.flatnonzero(live_cliff) # every state a decision is made in
n_rows_cliff, n_cols_cliff = cliff.shape
cliff_cells = [(n_rows_cliff - 1) * n_cols_cliff + col for col in range(1, n_cols_cliff - 1)]
v_star_cliff, q_star_cliff = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF)
pi_random = np.ones((cliff.n_states, cliff.n_actions)) / cliff.n_actions
v_random, q_random = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, pi_random)
optimal_cliff = q_star_cliff >= v_star_cliff[:, None] - TIE_TOLERANCE  # the optimal actions of each state

def induced_policy(actions, roots, env):
    """Turn the actions a planner chose into a policy table pi(a|s).

    A decision-time planner is run several times from each state. The induced policy picks
    each action with the fraction of those runs that chose it. In states where the planner
    was never run, it is uniform.

    Parameters
    ----------
    actions : array_like of int, shape (n_calls,)
        The action chosen by each planner call.
    roots : array_like of int, shape (n_calls,)
        The state each call planned from.
    env : Env
        Supplies the table sizes.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        pi(a|s). Each row sums to 1.
    """
    pi = np.zeros((env.n_states, env.n_actions))
    np.add.at(pi, (roots, actions), 1.0)
    pi[pi.sum(axis=1) == 0] = 1.0 / env.n_actions # Uniform
    return pi / pi.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def greedy_ties_split(q, env):
    """Return the greedy policy of q, with ties split evenly.

    An action is tied for best when its value is within TIE_TOLERANCE of the largest legal
    value. Each tied action gets an equal share of the probability.

    Parameters
    ----------
    q : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        Action values.
    env : Env
        Supplies the legal actions.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        pi(a|s). Each row sums to 1.
    """
    q_legal = np.where(env.legal_actions > 0, q, NEG_INF)
    best = q_legal >= q_legal.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) - TIE_TOLERANCE
    return best / best.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def grade(pi):
    """Grade a policy on the cliff exactly, with the DP oracle.

    Parameters
    ----------
    pi : ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The policy, as pi(a|s).

    Returns
    -------
    dict
        - "start": v_pi(S), the value of the start state.
        - "shortfall": the mean over the live states of v_*(s) - v_pi(s). 0 is optimal.
        - "optimal": the mean over the live states of the probability pi puts on optimal
          actions. 1 is optimal.
    """
    v, _ = exact(cliff, GAMMA_CLIFF, pi)
    return dict(
        start=v[start_cliff],
        shortfall=(v_star_cliff - v)[live_cliff].mean(),
        optimal=(pi * optimal_cliff).sum(axis=1)[live_cliff].mean()
    )

The random policy in this experiment is terrible: \(v(S) = -261\), because along the bottom row a quarter of its moves step off the cliff.
One step of greedy lookahead on its values (which is one step of policy iteration) is an enormous improvement, bringing it up to \(-20\). But look at what that policy actually does (the top panel of the figure above). On the left half of the board it walks up into the top-left corner, whereas on the right half it runs along the top row into the top-right corner, and in both places it stays, pushing into the wall forever. \(-20 = -1/(1-0.95)\) is exactly the value of never finishing; \(-1\) on every step, discounted forever. Only the four cells beside the goal actually lead into it.
The issue is \(v_{\text{random}}\) itself. Under the random policy the goal is so far away that it barely affects the values, while the cliff dominates every state near it. So the values effectively say, get away from the cliff. The one-step lookahead does exactly that, and hides in a corner. The knowledge the planners start from is actively misleading, and each decision-time planner has to overcome it by looking ahead.






Warning



greedy_ties_split gives actions that are exactly tied for best equal probability, as the Dyna agents did, rather than handing every tie to action 0. With one step of lookahead only two states have ties, so it barely matters yet. But it will in later sections.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
The tree, level by level
With 4 actions and only deterministic moves, the states at depth \(k\) of the tree, for every root, fit in an array of shape (n_roots, 4^k). Building the next level is one lookup in the successor table followed by a reshape. To back up a level we add the rewards then reshape to (n_roots, 4^{k-1}, 4) so that each node’s four children sit together, and take the max over the last axis.
There is no scan here, because a scan needs every step to have the same shape, and each level of the tree has a different one. So the loop over levels is an ordinary Python loop that builds the graph one level at a time, and the depth \(d\) is fixed when the function is built.

def make_heuristic_search(env, depth, V_leaf, gamma):
    """Compile an exhaustive depth-d lookahead tree, for a batch of roots in a deterministic env.

    The tree holds every action sequence of length ``depth`` from the root, n_actions^depth
    leaves in all. Each leaf is valued by the heuristic ``V_leaf``. Values are then backed
    up one level at a time, toward the root:

        value(node) = max over legal a of [ r(node, a) + gamma * value(child after a) ].

    At the root the max is not taken, so the root keeps one backed-up value per action.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        A deterministic environment. Its next state is read as ``P.argmax(axis=2)``.
    depth : int
        Number of levels of actions in the tree. 1 is the one-step lookahead.
    V_leaf : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        The heuristic value of each state, used at the leaves.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(roots) -> (best_action, root_values)``, with ``roots`` of shape (n_roots,).
        ``best_action`` has shape (n_roots,) and ``root_values`` (n_roots, n_actions).
    """
    next_state = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.P.argmax(axis=2))
    reward = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.reward_mean)
    legal = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    V = pt.as_tensor_variable(V_leaf)
    roots = pt.lvector("roots")
    n_roots = roots.shape[0]

    levels = [roots[:, None]] # (n_roots, 1), (n_roots, 4), (n_roots, 16) ...
    for _ in range(depth):
        levels.append(next_state[levels[-1]].reshape((n_roots, -1)))

    value = V[levels[-1]] # the heuristic, at the leaves
    for k in range(depth - 1, -1, -1): # back up one level at a time
        s = levels[k]
        backed_up_values = reward[s] + gamma * value.reshape((n_roots, -1, env.n_actions))
        backed_up_values = pt.where(legal[s] > 0, backed_up_values, NEG_INF)
        value = backed_up_values.max(axis=-1) if k > 0 else backed_up_values[:, 0, :]
    return pytensor.function([roots], [value.argmax(axis=-1), value])

def lookahead_by_value_iteration(V, depth):
    """Compute the depth-d tree's root values without building the tree, on the cliff.

    A depth-d tree backs up d levels from V. That is the same as d - 1 sweeps of value
    iteration starting from V, followed by one more one-step lookahead
    ``q(s, a) = r(s, a) + gamma * v(s')`` that keeps every action. This gives the root
    values for every state at once, at a cost that grows with d instead of 4^d.

    Parameters
    ----------
    V : ndarray, shape (n_states,)
        The heuristic value of each state.
    depth : int
        The depth of the tree being reproduced.

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray, shape (n_states, n_actions)
        The backed-up value of each action from each state, as the root of a depth-d tree.
    """
    _, _, action_values_of = ORACLE[cliff.name]
    v = V.copy()
    for _ in range(depth - 1):
        v = np.where(cliff.terminal, 0.0, action_values_of(v, GAMMA_CLIFF).max(axis=1))
    return action_values_of(v, GAMMA_CLIFF)


check_rows = []
for depth in (1, 2, 4, 6, 8):
    search = make_heuristic_search(cliff, depth, v_random, GAMMA_CLIFF)
    _, root_values = search(roots_cliff)
    difference = np.abs(root_values - lookahead_by_value_iteration(v_random, depth)[roots_cliff]).max()
    check_rows.append(dict(depth=depth, leaves=cliff.n_actions ** depth, difference=difference))
tree_check = pd.DataFrame(check_rows)

tree_check_table = (
    GT(tree_check, rowname_col="depth")
    .tab_header(

    )

    )

    .fmt_scientific(columns="difference", decimals=1)
    .cols_align("right", columns=["leaves", "difference"])

    )
    .tab_footnote(

        f"{cliff.n_actions} root actions. 0.0 means the two agree to the last bit.",
        loc.column_labels(columns="difference")
    )

The tree and value iteration agree exactly at every depth. So from here on we can use whichever form is cheaper. The check above built trees for all 37 roots at once, up to depth 8 (2.4 million leaves in total). The table below uses the value-iteration form at every depth, and as a spot check we also build two literal trees from the start state alone: depth 11 and depth 12, with 4.2 and 16.8 million leaves.
On the cliff every step costs \(-1\), which produces many tied actions. So the policy at each depth splits its probability evenly between the tied best actions (greedy_ties_split), just as the Dyna agents did.

ARROW_GLYPHS = {UP: "↑", DOWN: "↓", LEFT: "←", RIGHT: "→"}   # the four actions, drawn as arrows for tables

def per_action(values):
    """Format one value per action as "↑ −9.73, ↓ −10.25, ...", with a true minus sign."""
    return ", ".join(f"{ARROW_GLYPHS[a]} {v:.2f}".replace("-", "−") for a, v in enumerate(values))

graded_depth = {}
depth_rows = []
for depth in range(1, 15):
    q_lookahead = lookahead_by_value_iteration(v_random, depth)
    pi_lookahead = greedy_ties_split(q_lookahead, cliff)
    graded_depth[depth] = grade(pi_lookahead)
    in_tree = np.zeros(cliff.n_states, dtype=bool)
    frontier = np.array([start_cliff])

    for _ in range(depth):
        frontier = np.unique(cliff.P.argmax(axis=2)[frontier].ravel())
        in_tree[frontier] = True

    depth_rows.append(dict(
        depth=depth,
        leaves=cliff.n_actions ** depth,
        distinct=in_tree.sum(),
        tied=" ".join(ARROW_GLYPHS[a] for a in np.flatnonzero(pi_lookahead[start_cliff])),
        **graded_depth[depth]
    ))
search_by_depth = pd.DataFrame(depth_rows)

literal_trees = {} # depth -> the backed-up value of each action at S, from the literal tree
for depth in (11, 12):
    _, root_values = make_heuristic_search(cliff, depth, v_random, GAMMA_CLIFF)(np.array([start_cliff]))
    literal_trees[depth] = root_values[0]

Each extra level of lookahead helps, starting with the states nearest the goal. The mean shortfall falls as we increase depth, as expected. The first states to be fixed are the ones closest to the goal. A depth-\(d\) tree from a state within \(d\) steps of the goal can see the goal, and once it can, the leaf values’ fear of the cliff no longer decides anything. The start state is 13 steps from the goal, the farthest of all, so it is fixed last.
From depth 4 to depth 11, “up”, “down” and “left” at \(S\) all back up to exactly the same value (the literal depth-11 tree gives \(-90.08\) for all three). Every step on the cliff costs \(-1\), so a plan that wastes a step now and a plan that wastes a step later reach the same leaf with the same total. Until the tree reaches the cell above the goal (12 steps from \(S\)), wasting a step costs nothing the tree can see. At depth 12 it can, and “up” pulls clearly ahead with \(-61.72\) against \(-86.58\). This is why tie-breaking is really important here. Had we broken ties toward action 0, which happens to be “up”, depth 11 would have appeared to solve the start state when it had only guessed right. Splitting ties shows the real, gradual improvement instead, as more and more of the states downstream of \(S\) get fixed.
The cost grows exponentially. Depth 12 means 16.8 million leaves for a single decision, in a world with only 37 states. The tree visits the same states over and over, whereas value iteration merges them: it computed the same numbers for all 37 states in 11 sweeps. That is the downside of heuristic search on a tabular problem. It pays off when the state space is too big to sweep but the tree from the current state is still affordable. When the whole table fits in memory, as it does here, search loses.

title: Planning and Learning with Tabular Methods
text:
A tree in fixed-size arrays
A tree is normally built from pointers, with nodes added one at a time, but a scan needs arrays whose shapes never change. The way around this is to notice that a tree growing by one node per iteration can never have more than n_iterations + 1 nodes. So we allocate arrays of that size up front, one tree per root, and fill them in as the tree grows:

node_state[tree, m]: the state at node \(m\) of a tree
children[tree, m, a]: the node that action \(a\) leads to from node \(m\), or \(-1\) if that action has not been expanded yet
N[tree, m, a] and W[tree, m, a]: the visit count and the summed returns for each edge.

Each of the four steps then becomes an array operation, done for every tree at once:

Selection is an inner scan over depth that walks down every tree together. It carries the current node and an active flag, which switches off once a tree reaches an unexpanded action or a terminal state, and it outputs the path each tree took.
Expansion writes one new entry into children and one into node_state.
Simulation reuses random_rollout_returns from the previous section.
Backup walks back along the path from the leaf to work out the return seen from each edge, then adds them all in at once with a single inc_subtensor. That is safe because a path never uses the same edge twice, and the padding after a path ends only adds zeros.

The exploration constant \(c\) has to match the size of the returns, which here range from about \(-10\) to \(-350\). We tried \(c \in \{30, 100, 300, 1000\}\) and settled on 300.

def make_mcts(env, gamma, horizon, max_depth, n_iterations, c, seed):
    """Compile Monte Carlo tree search with UCB, one tree per root.

    Each iteration in every tree at once:

    1. Selection: from the root, follow the tree. At a node with an untried legal action,
       stop and pick one of those at random. Otherwise pick the action with the largest
       upper confidence bound,

           W(m, a) / N(m, a) + c * sqrt( ln(sum_b N(m, b)) / N(m, a) ),

       where N counts visits of edge (m, a) and W sums their returns.
    2. Expansion: add one node for the untried action's next state.
    3. Simulation: a random rollout of ``horizon`` steps from that state.
    4. Backup: add 1 to N and the discounted return from that edge on to W, for every edge
       on the path.

    The trees live in fixed-size arrays with room for ``n_iterations + 1`` nodes, since
    each iteration adds at most one node. Node 0 is the root.

    Parameters
    ----------
    env : Env
        The environment, used as a sample model.
    gamma : float
        Discount factor.
    horizon : int
        Steps per rollout.
    max_depth : int
        The most selection steps per iteration.
    n_iterations : int
        Iterations per tree.
    c : float
        Exploration constant of the upper confidence bound.
    seed : int
        Seed for the shared random generator.

    Returns
    -------
    pytensor.compile.function.types.Function
        ``f(roots) -> (best_action, N_root, mean_return)``, with ``roots`` of shape
        (n_trees,). ``best_action`` is the most-visited root action, shape (n_trees,).
        ``N_root`` and ``mean_return = W / N`` at the root have shape (n_trees, n_actions).
    """
    P, reward, not_terminal, n_actions = tensors = environment_tensors(env)
    legal = pt.as_tensor_variable(env.legal_actions)
    rng_shared = pt.random.shared_rng(seed=seed, name="rng_mcts")
    roots = pt.lvector("roots")
    n_trees = roots.shape[0]
    capacity = n_iterations + 1
    trees = pt.arange(n_trees)

    def select(rng, node, active, expand_node, expand_action, leaf, children, node_state, N, W):
        """One level of the selection descent, in every tree at once.

        Parameters
        ----------
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        node : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The node each tree's descent is at.
        active : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 while the descent is still going; 0.0 once it has stopped.
        expand_node, expand_action : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The edge to expand, once the descent finds one.
        leaf : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The state the rollout will start from.
        children : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees, capacity, n_actions)
            The node each edge leads to, or -1 if the edge is not in the tree yet.
        node_state : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees, capacity)
            The environment state of each node.
        N, W : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees, capacity, n_actions)
            Visit counts and summed returns of each edge.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, node_next, active, expand_node, expand_action, leaf
            The carried values for the next level.
        node, a : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            The edge taken at this level.
        reward : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            Its reward, or 0 if the edge is not on the path.
        on_path : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 if this level's edge is part of the path.
        expanding : TensorVariable, shape (n_trees,)
            1.0 if this level's edge is the one being expanded.
        """
        s = node_state[trees, node]
        at_terminal = 1.0 - not_terminal[s]
        untried = pt.lt(children[trees, node], 0) * legal[s] # -1 for not expanded yet
        has_untried = pt.gt(untried.sum(axis=1), 0)

        # the 1e-12 keeps the probabilities defined when nothing is untried; that draw is then unused
        rng, a_new = rng.categorical(p=(untried + 1e-12) / (untried + 1e-12).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))
        visits = N[trees, node]
        ucb = W[trees, node] / visits + c * pt.sqrt(pt.log(visits.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / visits)
        a = pt.where(has_untried, a_new, pt.where(legal[s] > 0, ucb, NEG_INF).argmax(axis=1))
        on_path = active * (1.0 - at_terminal) # (node, a) is an edge of this path
        expanding = on_path * has_untried
        rng, s_next = rng.categorical(p=P[s, a])
        expand_node = pt.where(expanding > 0, node, expand_node)
        expand_action = pt.where(expanding > 0, a, expand_action)
        leaf = pt.where(active > 0, pt.where(expanding > 0, s_next, s), leaf)
        stop = pt.maximum(at_terminal, has_untried.astype("float64"))
        node_next = pt.where(active * (1.0 - stop) > 0, children[trees, node, a], node)
        return (
            rng,
            node_next,
            active * (1.0 - stop),
            expand_node,
            expand_action,
            leaf,
            node,
            a,
            on_path * reward[s, a],
            on_path,
            expanding
        )

    def iteration(i, rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes):
        """One MCTS iteration in every tree: selection, expansion, simulation, backup.

        Parameters
        ----------
        i : TensorVariable of int, scalar
            The iteration number. Unused.
        rng : RandomGeneratorSharedVariable
            The random generator state, threaded through the scan.
        children, node_state, N, W
            The trees, as described in `select`.
        n_nodes : TensorVariable of int, shape (n_trees,)
            Nodes in each tree so far. The next new node gets this index.

        Returns
        -------
        rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes
            The advanced generator and the grown trees.
        """
        zeros = pt.zeros((n_trees,), dtype="int64")

        # 1. selection
        (rng, _, _, expand_node_seq, expand_action_seq, leaf_seq,
         path_node, path_action, path_reward, on_path, expanding) = pytensor.scan(
            fn=select,
            outputs_info=[
                rng,
                zeros,
                pt.ones((n_trees,)),
                zeros,
                zeros,
                node_state[:, 0],
                None, None, None, None, None
            ],
            non_sequences=[children, node_state, N, W],
            n_steps=max_depth,
            return_updates=False
        )

        expand_node, expand_action, leaf = expand_node_seq[-1], expand_action_seq[-1], leaf_seq[-1]

        # 2. expansion
        expanded = expanding.sum(axis=0)
        children = pt.set_subtensor(
            children[trees, expand_node, expand_action],
            pt.where(expanded > 0, n_nodes, children[trees, expand_node, expand_action])
        )

        node_state = pt.set_subtensor(
            node_state[trees, n_nodes],
            pt.where(expanded > 0, leaf, node_state[trees, n_nodes])
        )

        n_nodes = n_nodes + expanded.astype("int64")

        # 3. simulation
        rng, G_leaf = random_rollout_returns(rng, leaf, tensors, gamma, horizon)

        # 4. backup: each edge's return, deepest first, then one scatter-add for the whole path
        def one_level_up(r, edge, G):
            "the return from one edge up: r + gamma * G on the path, unchanged off it"
            return pt.where(edge > 0, r + gamma * G, G)

        G_path = pytensor.scan(
            fn=one_level_up,
            sequences=[path_reward[::-1], on_path[::-1]],
            outputs_info=G_leaf,
            return_updates=False
        )
        G_path = G_path[::-1] # Reverse

        N = pt.inc_subtensor(N[trees[None, :], path_node, path_action], on_path)
        W = pt.inc_subtensor(W[trees[None, :], path_node, path_action], on_path * G_path)
        return rng, children, node_state, N, W, n_nodes

    rng_final, _, _, N_seq, W_seq, _ = pytensor.scan(
        fn=iteration,
        sequences=pt.arange(n_iterations),
        outputs_info=[
            rng_shared,
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions), dtype="int64") - 1,
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity), dtype="int64") + roots[:, None],
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions)),
            pt.zeros((n_trees, capacity, n_actions)),
            pt.ones((n_trees,), dtype="int64")
        ],
        return_updates=False
    )
    N_root, W_root = N_seq[-1][:, 0], W_seq[-1][:, 0]
    return pytensor.function(
        [roots],
        [N_root.argmax(axis=1), N_root, W_root / N_root],
        updates={rng_shared: rng_final}
    )

We run eight independent trees from every state, 296 trees in one batch, at four budgets, from 50 iterations (a tree of 51 nodes) up to 3,200.

C_UCB, MAX_DEPTH_MCTS, K_MCTS = 300, 30, 8

for n_iterations in (50, 200, 800, 3200):

Three steps from the goal, MCTS has found the way along the edge. 3,149 of the 3,200 visits went right, and its estimate for that move, \(-12.3\), is most of the way from what random rollouts alone would say (\(q_{\text{random}} = -190.5\)) to the true value (\(q_* = -2.9\)). The tree has grown along the edge all the way to the goal, so every iteration down that branch now reaches the goal within a few steps, instead of handing over to a random walk beside the cliff.
Eight steps from the goal, it’s a different story “Up” gets 2,356 of the visits, and every action’s mean return lies between \(-139\) and \(-352\). That is an order of magnitude away from \(q_*\), and about the same size as \(q_{\text{random}}\), implying that no iteration has yet followed the edge far enough to reach the goal before the random rollout took over.
The rollouts here are deceptive, not just noisy. From any cell next to the cliff, a random walk falls off a quarter of the time, so the edge looks catastrophic. The tree policy sensibly spends its visits away from the edge. However, that is exactly where the tree would have to grow to learn otherwise.
The averaging in the backup makes this trap hard to escape. An edge’s value is the mean of every return that has ever passed through it, so the early, terrible rollout returns keep dragging down the path along the edge until enough good returns outnumber them. That is also why even the successful estimate above, \(-12.3\), is still short of the true \(-2.9\).

The figure above puts all three planners on one axis, computation per decision, and on that axis heuristic search looks absurdly cheap: depth 5 (1,364 tree nodes) beats MCTS at 3,200 iterations (around 480,000 simulated transitions). But this is not a like-for-like comparison:

Heuristic search was given \(v_{\text{random}}\) exactly, at every leaf, for free. Computing it took a full DP solve on the distribution model (background planning) before the first decision was ever made.
The rollout algorithm and MCTS had only a sample model. They had to estimate the same values by running the random policy, one noisy 150-step return at a time.

The benefits of decision-time planning depends on the knowledge it starts from. With a decent value function, a shallow search goes a long way. Without one, simulation has to pay for that knowledge, and the rollout policy decides whether the simulations even point in the right direction. On the cliff, random rollouts point the wrong way near the edge, so MCTS is only a middling planner here. Its strength is growing a tree toward promising path when rollouts are at least roughly informative. Its weakness, which we have just measured, is that averaged rollout returns can hide a good path behind a first step that looks dangerous.
